Diesel (Regulation of Supply and Distribution and P revention of Malpractices) Amendment Order, 
2008. 
 
GENERAL OBSERVATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
  
28. The Committee observes that financial incentive s arising from differences in prices are 
generally the primary cause of fuel adulteration.  Adulteration of gasoline & diesel is indulged 
primarily due to the significant price difference b etween these products and the adulterant.  
Hence, there is need to establish a monitoring regi me and system of fines that can act as a 
strong deterrent to fuel adulteration.  
 
 29.  Adulteration of transport fuels at the point of sale and transportation has become a 
routine problem in India. There are several petrole um products available in the country, 
which are close substitute of gasoline and diesel, but are available at considerable lower 

prices.  While a number of analytical techniques ar e available to detect adulteration, it is 
important to have good sampling technique and acces s to a good petroleum analytical 
laboratory.   
 
 30. Consumer interest is the prime objective of th e quality surveillance program.  
Consumer representatives groups such as consumer fo rum, NGOs, representative from the 
local Transport Authority, Civil Supplies Departmen t, Bureau of Indian Standards and 
Pollution Control Boards/ Agencies may be involved to take up the sample collection and 
surveillance activity.  This can be achieved by a c redible monitoring system and   appropriate 
surveillance programs. 
 
31. Government/ OMCs should ensure that specific no rms and guidelines are in place with 
regard to all activities and operations of the indu stry including retailers, traders, transporters 
and oil companies to curb adulteration.  Marketing Discipline Guidelines in vogue should be 
regularly modified /revised in view of the changing scenario to make them more effective. 
 
32. In the view of the Committee, guidelines regard ing grant of authorization to market 
transportation fuel should be specific and have cla rity with regard to all technicalities 
pertaining to provisions for performance guarantee and bank guarantee so as to leave no 
scope for any kind of arbitration and discretion an d, accordingly, recommends to the 
Ministry/ Regulatory Board to take immediate/ neces sary action in this regard to ensure the 
same.   
 
33. Inspections by joint teams of Anti-Adulteration  Cell and State Pollution Control 
Boards officials should be taken up. 
 
34. Policy for imposing severe penalty and punishme nt to the adulterators needs to be 
imbibed into the legal framework to discourage adul teration. Penalty system should be severe 
and imposed upstream. In case of an abuse in fuel m arket, the penalty should be imposed on 
all concerned along the supply chain, i.e.  the company, transporters and dealers. 
                                                                                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                

35. A culture of “Good Business” needs to be develo ped/ re-enforced within the industry to 
eradicate adulteration via  awareness-raising by Government organizations and greater effort 
by State Governments to monitor and enforce regulations. 
 
36. There is need to prevent en-route adulteration of Motor Spirit and High Speed Diesel 
by transportation /tank truck crew. In this regard feasibility of replacing the existing sealing 
system for the tanks carrying MS/HSD with other Security locking system may be explored. 
 
37. Government should expedite the installation of Global Positioning System (GPS) to 
monitor the movement of tank trucks.  The Committee  feels that installing GPS should be 
made mandatory and the same be operationalized at the earliest. 
 
38. Petrol pump owners should be motivated for good  & quality conscious business 
through a regular and routine monitoring system.   
 
39. Government should interact and coordinate with the Oil Companies and manufactures 
for upgradation  of the dispensing units to obviate the possibility of short delivery. 
 
40. Sampling system/ procedure should be such that it brings greater transparency at 
various levels in the whole process right from the filling point up to the retail outlet.  Also, 
provision for on-site testing facilities including number of Mobile Laboratories needs to be 
increased. 
 
41. The Committee appreciates that the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas are aware 
of their duty and the need and importance of lying the statutory rules/ regulations/orders and 
Annual Reports before each House of Parliament. The  Committee expects that the Ministry 
would continue to adhere to the timely framing and laying of the notifications/ Annual 
Reports   in future also. 
  
42. Companies should design and provide a system at  their Retail Outlets (ROs), which is 
robust, rugged and scalable on a long-term basis to  accommodate all the new technological 
advancements in retail of petroleum.  The Committee  recommends that all the OMGs should 

have a time bound programme to complete the process  of automation for all their retail 
outlets which would be a significant step in curbin g the malpractices at the dispensing units 
effectively. 

II  
Report  
on 
The Electrical Wires, Cables, Appliances and Protection Devices and Accessories (Quality 
Control) Order, 2003 
 
The Government framed the Electrical Wires, Cables,  Appliances and Protection Devices 
and Accessories (Quality Control) Order, 2003 (Annexure-I) under Section 14 of the Bureau of 
Indian Standards Act, 1986 rescinding  the General Service Electric Lamps (Quality 
Control)Order,1989 and the Electrical Wires, Cables , Appliances  and Accessories (Quality 
Control) Order,1993 issued by erstwhile Ministry of  Industry (Department of Industrial 
Development).The Order was notified in the Gazette of India on 17 th  February, 2003 with the 
objective to ensure the quality of the electrical w ires,  cables, appliances, protection devices and 
accessories and to fulfill this objective the appro priate authority has been entrusted with appropriate 
powers.  
 
2. During the course of examination of the Order, t he Committee held three meetings.  The 
Committee held discussions with the representatives  of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry 
(Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion), Mi nistry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public 
Distribution (Department of Consumer Affairs) and B ureau of Indian Standards.  Views/ 
suggestions on the efficacy of the said Order were also received from organizations/ associations/ 
manufactures like  (i) Electrical Lamp & Component Manufacturers Association of India, (ii) Indo 
Asian Fusegear Limited, (iii) Federation of Industr ies of India, (iv) Indian Society of Lighting 
Engineers and (v) Infopower.  The Electrical Wires,  Cables, Appliances and Accessories (Quality 
Control) Order, 1993 has since been amended four ti mes on 5.2.2004, 22.8.2005, 19.2.2009 and 
7.8.2009 respectively.  
 
3. The Committee on Subordinate Legislation took up  the said Quality Control Order, 2003 for 
detailed examination and a detailed questionnaire o n the subject was forwarded to the Ministry of 
Commerce and Industry (Department of Industrial Pol icy and Promotion) for 
comments/clarifications on 11 
th  May, 2004. The Ministry furnished their replies on  8 th  September, 

2004 (Annexure-II).  The points raised by the Committee and the replies of the Ministry thereon 
are given in the succeeding paragraphs. 
 
4. The Committee wanted to know whether the Electri cal Wires, Cables, Appliances and 
Protection Devices and Accessories (Quality Control) Order, 2003 had been laid on the Table of the 
both Houses of Parliament, if so, the details there of. The Ministry informed that the said Order, 
2003 had been laid on the Table of both the Houses of Parliament vide  
OM No.6(9)/2001-LEI dated 
5th  March,2003.  
 
5. The Bureau of Indian Standards Act was enacted i n 1986 whereas the Electrical Wires, 
Cables, Appliances and Protection Devices and Acces sories (Quality Control) Order has been 
enacted in the year 2003. The Committee inquired ab out the reasons for delay in the enactment of 
the Order and in what manner the areas governed by the Order were being regulated so far.  The 
Ministry replied that BIS Act was enacted in 1986 t o strengthen the work on standard formulation 
and certification in national interest. It being a continuous process, Quality Control Orders were 
being issued by Government of India under this Act from time to time with a view to protect the 
interests of common consumer. Earlier 7 electrical products were covered in Quality Control 
(Orders) No. GSR 463(E), dated 24 
th  April, 1989 and GSR 83(E), dated 24 February, 1993  issued 
under Essential Commodities Act. Due to deletion of  these 7 items from the list of essential 
commodities, the new Electrical Wires, Cables, Appl iances and Protection Devices and Accessories 
Quality Control (Order), 2003 was issued on 17 th  February, 2003 under BIS Act.  
 
6. Clause 1(2 ) states “ In respect of items covered under serial numbers 1 to 7 of the Schedule, 
this Order shall come into force with immediate eff ect. In respect of items covered under serial 
numbers 8 to 24 of the Schedule, this Order shall c ome into force after a period of six months from 
the date of publication in the Official Gazette .”   The Committee asked about the different time 
schedules for different items and the criteria for fixing the time schedule.  The Ministry informed 
that item numbers 1 to 7 were earlier covered under  mandatory certification vide 
 Quality Control 
(Order) issued under Essential Commodity Act. Since , they were already in operation under 
mandatory certification; it was felt that no time p eriod would be required for implementation of the 
Order in respect of these items. The said Order, th erefore, came into force with immediate effect. 

However, for the remaining items at Sl Nos. 8 to 24 being brought under mandatory certification for 
the first time, time period of six months was considered necessary for implementation.  
 
7. Clause 2(f) defines “manufacturer”, in relation to electrical wires, ca bles, appliances, 
protection, devices and accessories, means a person  who, or a firm or a Hindu undivided family 
which produces, makes, assembles or manufactures an y such electrical wires, cables, appliances, 
protection devices and accessories and includes a p erson who, or a firm or Hindu undivided family 
which claims such electrical wires, cables, applian ces, protection devices and accessories to be 
produced, made, assembled or ‘manufactured’ by such person or firm or Hindu undivided family as 
the case may be.”  The Committee wanted to know the justification for  including within the 
definition of the term manufacturer such persons si mply on the basis of their ‘claim’. The Ministry 
replied that the definition of manufacturer includes any person who ‘claims’ to be the manufacturer. 
The same is also given in the Consumer Protection A ct, 1986 and the Standards of Weights and 
Measures Act, 1978.  
 
8. Clause 3(1) states “Prohibition regarding manufacture, storage, sale an d distribution, etc:  
(1) No person shall by himself or through any perso n on his behalf manufacture or stores for sale, 
sell, or distribute any electrical wires, cables, a ppliances, protection devices and accessories which  
do not conform to the Specified Standards and do no t bear Standard Mark of the Bureau on 
obtaining certification marks licence:” The Committee inquired about the standard specifica tions 
prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) in comparison with the international standards 
and the objectives sought to be achieved by prescri bing that the specifications given by the foreign 
buyers “shall not in any case be less than the spec ified standard”. The Committee was apprehensive 
that Indian standards may be inferior to standards fixed by other countries. The Committee also 
noted that though organizations like WTO specified standards seemingly to encourage competition, 
unifying the standards all over the world for maint enance of healthy market conditions, this usually 
led to arm-twisting and notching the markets of the  developing countries. The Committee, 
accordingly, wanted to know about the Quality Control measures adopted and prescribed by Central 
Government for the manufacturing sector in the area s of stiff competition.  Also, if there was a 
scope for Central Government to directly adopt inte rnational specifying standards instead of 
standards specified by Bureau of Indian Standards f or exportable goods.  India being a signatory to 

WTO accord, the Committee inquired whether the Cent ral Government adhered to international 
standards in case of importable goods.  
 
9. In response the Ministry informed that internati onal standards namely, ISO 9002, 9003 etc 
were generic standards for Quality Management Syste ms and these were not product standards. 
Corresponding Indian Standards for Quality Systems are totally identical with the international 
standards. It was further apprised that most of the Indian Standards on products were either identical 
or based on corresponding International Standards a nd they had been brought under mandatory 
certification as their quality may affect health an d safety of the consumers. The Committee noted 
the reply of the Ministry that the standard making process followed in BIS was transparent and 
equally applicable for Indian manufacturers of elec trical goods as well as foreign manufacturers 
exporting items to India.  In India certain product s have been brought under mandatory certification 
of BIS which is evenly applicable for Indian manufa cturers as well as foreign manufacturers 
exporting to India.  Moreover, these standards are in line with WTO agreement.   
 
10. Clause 3(2)  states “The sub-standard or defective electrical wires, ca bles, appliances, 
protection devices and accessories or raw–material or components, which do not conform to the 
Specified Standard shall be deformed by the manufac turer beyond use and disposed of as scrap 
within three months.”  The Committee wanted to know if there existed any s upervisory authority or 
Agency to oversee that manufacturers were complying  with the provisions of deformation and 
disposal of their goods which did not conform to th e Specified Standard. The Committee also 
inquired about the role of the Central Government i n this regard. The Ministry stated that according 
to the Quality Control Order, 2003, BIS had been co nferred the sole authority to issue license to 
manufacturers for marking their products complying with Indian Standards. As per the Order, 
appropriate authority appointed by respective State  Governments was responsible for implementing 
this Order and were authorized to take action wherever non-compliance is observed. 
 
11. Clause 4(4) states  “Consequent to the expiry of any license or cancell ation thereof by the 
Bureau for one or more of the electrical wires, cab les, appliances, protection devices and 
accessories mentioned in Column (2) of the Schedule , the Appropriate Authority shall also be 
informed of the same by the Bureau .”  The Committee, accordingly, desired to know the  objective 

behind providing information regarding expiry/cance llation of license by the Bureau to the 
Appropriate Authority and if the Appropriate Author ity was the implementing authority for the 
Order, the type of information maintained by the Ap propriate Authority alongwith the mechanism 
in place for ensuring regular updating of the same.  The Ministry informed that the implementing 
authority for this Order included various State Gov ernment Agencies. However, authority for 
issuing the license to use BIS standard mark on the  product or expiry/ cancellation of BIS license 
lies with BIS only.  Therefore, it is necessary to provide the requisite information to ensure effective 
implementation of the Order 
 
12. Clause 5(c) states  “enter and search any premises and seize  any  electrical wires, cables, 
appliances, protection devices and accessories in r espect of which it has reason to believe that a 
contravention of this Order has been committed or t he said electrical wires, cables, appliances, 
protection devices and accessories are not of the S pecified Standard ”  The Committee was of the 
view that the words “in respect of which it has reason to believe that a contravention of this 
Order has been committed”  were ambiguous in nature and that there should be some safeguards 
in place to prevent undue harassment of any dealer or manufacturer. The Ministry informed that the 
provision given in the Order is considered necessar y with a view to prosecute whenever any 
contravention is observed. However, those provision s were already there in the earlier Quality 
Control (Order) which was enacted under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. 
 
13. Clause 9 deals with  obligation to furnish information and states  “No manufacturer or dealer 
shall with intent to evade the provisions of this O rder, refuse to give any information lawfully 
demanded from him under Clause 5 or conceal, destroy, mutilate or deface any books or documents 
or any electrical wires, cables, appliances, protec tion devices and accessories kept by, or in the 
possession or control of, such person.”   The Committee wanted to know about the liability of  the 
manufacturer for not furnishing the information and  penal provisions for them who resort to 
concealing, destroying or mutilating books/documents/information.  The Ministry submitted that the 
penalties for violation of any provision of the Qua lity Control Order which had been notified 
under Section 14 of BIS Act shall be the same as given in Section 33 of BIS Act. 
 

14. The Committee noted that the objective of the Q uality Control Order, 2003 is to ensure the 
quality of the electrical wires  cables, appliances, protection devices and accessor ies and for which 
the appropriate authority has been entrusted with a ppropriate powers. The Committee, accordingly, 
wanted to know  the extent to which the objective of the Order has been achieved and adequacy of 
machinery both at the level of Central Government a nd the State Governments for ensuring 
compliance with the Order.  The Committee further w anted to know to what extent buyers or 
general public can be associated in the implementation of the Order.  
 
15. The Ministry informed that before the enforceme nt of the Electrical Wires, Cables, 
Appliances and Protection Devices and Accessories ( Quality Control) Order- 2003, the Ministry of 
Industry (Department of Industrial Development) iss ued the General Service Electric Lamps 
(Quality Control) Order, 1989 and the Electrical Wi res, Cables, Appliances and Protection Devices 
and Accessories (Quality Control) Order, 1993 under  the Section 3 of the Essential Commodities 
Act, 1955. Hence, sufficient experience was gathere d during the process of implementation of 
mandatory certification in the country and various stakeholders including common consumers, 
NGOs and relevant industry groups were consulted be fore the notification of the Electrical Wires, 
Cables, Appliances and Protection Devices and Acces sories (Quality Control) Order,2003  was 
issued. 
 
16. The Committee considered the matter in its meet ing on 5 
th  September, 2005 and decided to 
seek the views of leading traders/manufacturers’ as sociations connected with the subject matter, so 
as to have inputs on the efficacy of the Quality Co ntrol Order, 2003. Views/ suggestions were 
received from (i) Electrical Lamp & Component Manuf acturers Association of India, (ii) Indo 
Asian Fusegear Limited, (iii) Federation of Industr ies of India, (iv) Indian Society of Lighting 
Engineers and (v) Infopower and were duly considere d by the Committee.  Views/ suggestions so 
received have been enumerated below: 
(i) The said Quality Control Order has been issued by Government keeping in view the adverse 
impact of large-scale imports of spurious electrica l goods and to safeguard the interests of the 
Indian consumers.  As a result of expansion in powe r generation and distribution in hand, the 
demand for electrical equipment such as switches, w ires and CFL’s etc. has gone up many fold.  
Thus, quality of these electrical equipments needs to be controlled.  The Quality Control Order was 

supposed to come into force by August 2003 on all 2 4 products but unfortunately it was not fully 
implemented and in case of certain products such as  Compact Fluorescent Lamp (CFL) the 
implementation had been deferred till February 2007.  
 
(ii) BIS specifications lay special emphasis on tou gh conditions of performance for electrical 
products with regard to India. It is appropriate th at all electrical products to be used in India shou ld 
comply with Indian standard specifications to suit the Indian conditions properly.  
 
(iii) The BIS mark gives legal authority to BIS to cancel such BIS mark of such products, which 
are found not fully complying with the BIS specific ations even if such products are picked up from 
the open market.  BIS needs to take severe punitive  actions against manufacturers, importers or 
traders of sub-standard BIS marked products.   
  
(iv) There is need for effective protection of cons umer interest through BIS mark.  Closer 
coordination needs to be established between the Mi nistry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of 
Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution and State Governments to co-ordinate their efforts 
to protect the interests of the consumers and ensure that the objective of BIS mandatory certification 
mark are being effectively implemented.    
 
(v) For effective monitoring of proper use of BIS m ark by genuine licensees, BIS should 
encourage public awareness campaign through adverti sement and coverage by electronic and print 
media and by making presentations for the manufactu rers, Marketing Associations, Electronic 
Contractors and the general public.  Seminars and w orkshops could be organized and interest 
groups involved for full implementation and enforce ment and use by manufacturers, sellers and 
officials of BIS.   
  
(vi) Substantial man power should be made available  within BIS organization or services of 
private agency for effective monitoring needs to be supervised/ monitored. 
  

(vii) BIS Act may be amended suitably so as to vest  sufficient powers with the BIS to enable the 
organization to implement the Act without depending  much upon the State Governments for its 
implementation. 
 
(viii) Punishment as provided in the Act/ Rules is neither enough nor deterrent.  As such BIS Act 
should be suitably amended to allow BIS to impose s tringent penalties and punishments to the 
defaulters/ misusers of BIS Standards.        
  
 (ix) Bench marks as declared in BIS Citizens’ Char ter not being met.  While BIS has set bench 
marks for its various activities in its Citizens’ C harter, regular reviewing of the achievements of 
these bench marks is not being done.   
 
(x) BIS is using, generating and disposing hazardou s materials and resulting hazardous waste in 
violation of applicable rules/ regulations.  BIS is  using DG sets without acoustic enclosures in 
violation of Noise Laws. 
 
(xi) BIS has been mandated by Parliament for harmon ious development of standardization, but 
in the last few years BIS has refused to make stand ards when approached by other organizations 
needing standards for their working.  This has resu lted in many organizations formulating standards 
by themselves or through other agencies.  This has in reality defeated the basic purpose of 
establishing BIS  
  
17. The above views/ suggestions were forwarded to the Ministry of Commerce & Industry 
(Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion) for t heir comments/ clarifications.  In response, the 
Ministry submitted that adequate provisions exist i n clause 3 of the Quality Control Order, 2003 
read with section 14 and 33 of the BIS Act, 1986.  The Quality Control has been issued under 
section 14 of the BIS Act, 1980, and section 33(1) of the Act provides that any person who 
contravenes the provisions of the section 14 shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which 
may extend upto one year or with fine, which may ex tend upto Rs. 50,000 or both.  As regards the 
punitive aspects, the same have been taken care of in section 33(1) of the BIS Act. However, BIS 
have proposed amendments to BIS Act to modify vario us provisions. Further, BIS has started to 

outsource part of the work related to product certi fication scheme and enforcement.  Manpower is 
also being augmented through recruitment of officer s.  This initiative will help BIS to provide the 
services required by the industry effectively.  Reg arding the views on CFL, the Ministry submitted 
that through Electrical Wires, Cables, appliances a nd Protection Devices and Accessories (Quality 
Control) Amendment Order, 2005, Self Ballasted Lamp s for general lighting Services, known as 
CFLs were brought under mandatory certification whi ch came into force after 18 months from date 
of notification i.e. w.e.f. 22 nd  February, 2007.      
   
18. The Committee, thereafter, heard the representa tives of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, 
Food and Public Distribution (Department of Consume r Affairs), Ministry of Commerce and 
Industry (Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion) and the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) 
on the said Rules as well as on the working of BIS on 9 
th  April, 2010.  During the course of the 
meeting, the Committee raised the following issues: (i) why Quality Control Order, 2003 was issued 
by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotio n when it had no role in the implementation of 
the Order, (ii) when the BIS and BIS Act, 1986 came  under the administrative control of the 
Department of Consumer Affairs, (iii) reasons for r emoval of some electrical items from the 
purview of the Quality Control Order, 2003 and its resultant effect on the quality of such items.  
Whether the Committee had recommended that a Scient ist should be appointed as DG-BIS and if 
so, the reasons for not implementing the recommendations.    
 
 
19. Regarding Committee’s query on removal of certa in items, Ministry of Commerce and 
Industry (Department of Industrial Policy and Promo tion) replied that those electrical items were 
removed from the purview of the Quality Control Ord er, 2003 as they were not for direct 
consumption of the common man.  Infact, these elect rical items were internal  to the industrial use 
and really used in production of other products.   Quality Control Order, 2003 was issued bringing 
24 electrical items under mandatory BIS certificati on to protect the consumer from spurious items. 
Due to persistent request from the Industrial Assoc iations/BIS and after a series of meetings with 
them the Ministry in concurrence with the Ministry of Law took a unanimous decision to delete the 
seven items from the Order.  The Ministry had refer red the matter to the Indian Electrical and 
Electronics Manufacturer’s Association (IEEMA) on t he definition of ‘single use’ and ‘multiple 

use’.  Based on the advice tendered by IEEMA the Mi nistry confirmed that all the seven deleted 
items were of single use. The Ministry also informed that the papers of Quality Control Order, 2003 
were laid on the Table of the Lok sabha and Rajya S abha Secretariat on 13 th  March, 2003 and 21 st  
April, 2003 respectively. The deletion of 9 Household Electrical items from (Quality Control) Order 
was forwarded to Lok Sabha Secretariat and Rajya Sabha Secretariat on 9 th  July, 2004. 
 
20. The Committee further observed that for a number of  products like invertors, the 
quality standards had not been laid down and expres sed concern on certification and 
registration of such products for ensuring quality standards. The Committee was not satisfied 
with BIS’s reply in this regard.  It took note of the fact that BIS had already form ulated quality 
standard specification for soild state invertors run from storage batteries.  
 
21. The Committee also conveyed its concern regarding t he practice followed by BIS for 
issuing certification.  Earlier, ISI used to first inspect and examine the  company and its product and 
then registration was allowed. After that a new pra ctice started in which the company itself 
provided a certificate and BIS registered the produ cts. The Committee expressed concern that such 
a practice would lead to compromising of the qualit y standards of electrical goods as inspection by 
competent authorities had been dispersed with.  
 
22. The Ministry informed that the practice of carr ying out preliminary inspection and passing 
of samples in independent testing by BIS officers f or grant of license was still there.  In addition, a 
simplified procedure for grant of license has been introduced in order to reduce the time period for 
grant of licenses. Under the scheme, a visit is und ertaken either by a BIS officer or by a Charted 
Engineer to judge the competency of the applicant t o manufacture products in line with the 
requirements of the prescribed Indian Standard. In case, the Officer/ Charted Engineer gets satisfied 
that the applicant has the capacity to manufacture the product as per the specifications prescribed in  
the standards, the test report of the sample, as su bmitted by the applicant from any of the BIS 
approved laboratories, is accepted for consideratio n for grant of license. However, with the view to 
ensure that the sample meets the requirements of th e relevant Indian Standard, a sample is drawn 
during the visit and sent for independent testing a nd case is reviewed, if necessary, after receipt of  
test report of the sample. In case where  a license  has been granted based on the assessment of the 

Charted Engineer, BIS officers visit the premises o f the licensee within a month after grant of 
license and in addition to judging the capability o f the licensee, a sample is drawn for independent 
testing and follow up action is taken, if necessary  based on the test reports . This simplified 
procedure expedites the process of grant of license , but monitoring and control mechanism is still 
retained by BIS. 
 
23. The Committee then took up the Quality Control Order for discussion with the 
representatives of the Department of Policy and Pro motion, Department of Consumer Affairs, BIS 
and leading manufacturers/ traders of electrical it ems at Bangalore on 21 st  June, 2011. A study note 
(Annexure III ) was prepared.  During the course of discussion the Committee raised various  issues 
like (i) whether BIS have carried out amendments to  the BIS Act to impose stringent penalties to 
those who do not comply with the provisions of the Act; (ii)  steps taken to prevent and detect the 
manufacture or import of spurious electrical goods in the country; (iii) proposal, if any, to bring 
more electrical items under mandatory certification  and the opinion of manufacturers in this regard, 
(iv) whether BIS conducts regular inspections of fa ctories manufacturing electrical products and 
store-houses selling electrical products, and (v) the level of compliance by factories and traders with 
the quality prescribed by BIS and action taken agai nst the violators.  The Committee was informed 
that testing of electrical equipment is usually not  done in time and it takes a lot of time. The 
Committee observed the need to strengthen the staff  of BIS, to increase the number of BIS 
labs so as to reduce imbalances in the country in r espect of distribution of BIS laboratories 
and emphasized the need to strengthen the enforceme nt of rules.  The Committee noted the 
views of the Ministry for mandatory certification f or Chinese or foreign electrical goods 
imported to India along with deterrent and stringen t action to be taken for faking ISI marks. 
Some cases of outsourcing of testing also came to the notice of the Committee. 
 
GENERAL OBSERVATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
24. The Committee observed that when it was inquire d to the Ministry of Commerce and 
Industry (Department of Industrial Policy and Promo tion) whether subsequent amendments 
to the Electrical Wires, Cables, Appliances and Pro tection Devices and Accessories Quality 
Control Order, 2003 were laid before the Parliament  they could not provide a satisfactory 

reply. The Committee, therefore, reiterated that it  is mandatory for every 
rule/regulation/order issued by the Government unde r various Acts of the Parliament and 
their subsequent amendments to be laid on the Table of the House. 
25. The Committee observed that for a number of pro ducts like invertors, the quality 
standards had not been laid down and expressed conc ern on certification and registration of 
such products for ensuring quality standards. It to ok note of the fact that BIS had already 
formulated quality standard specification for solid  state invertors run from storage batteries.  
In the opinion of the Committee, BIS has been manda ted by Parliament for harmonious 
development of standardization.  However, a number of organizations were still awaiting 
standards for their working from BIS, which often r esulted in organizations formulating 
standards by themselves or through other agencies.  In the Committee’s opinion, this in 
reality, defeats the basic purpose of establishment of BIS itself.    
 
26. The Committee observes that Bureau of Indian St andards has not done much  to 
arouse mass awareness about quality standard specif ications of different electrical goods and 
devices which are either manufactured in India or i mported from foreign countries especially 
China and advises BIS to organize  public awareness  campaigns through advertisements and 
coverage  in  electronic and print media. 
 
27. The Committee observes the need to strengthen t he staff of BIS, to increase the 
number of BIS labs so as to reduce imbalances in th e country in respect of distribution of BIS 
laboratories and emphasizes the need to strengthen the enforcement of rules for mandatory 
certification of Chinese or foreign electrical good s imported to India along with deterrent and 
stringent action to be taken for faking ISI marks.  
 
28. The Committee observes that closer coordination  needs to be established between the 
Ministry of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Consumer Affairs and the States to co-ordinate 
their efforts to protect the interests of the consu mers towards ensuring that the objective of 
BIS mandatory certification mark is being effectively implemented, and,  by greater efforts by 
the States in taking quick punitive action against those importers or traders or manufacturers 

who produce or deal in sub-standard electrical equi pment which do not comply to BIS 
specifications.  
 
29. The Committee is not satisfied with the reply o f the Ministry on the point that Quality 
Control Order was supposed to come into force by Au gust 2003 on all 24 products but 
unfortunately it was not fully implemented and in c ase of certain products such as Compact 
Fluorescent Lamp (CFL) the implementation had been deferred till February 2007.   In the 
view of the Committee, delays in the enforcement of  rules adversely affect large sections of 
society.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends th at the Ministry should ensure that such 
instances of inordinate delay are avoided in future.      
  
30. For regular monitoring there is need to strengt hen vigilance by BIS.  Punishment is 
neither enough nor deterrent.  As such BIS Act shou ld be suitably amended to allow BIS to 
impose stringent penalties and punishments to the defaulters/ misusers of BIS Standards.        
 
31. The Committee expressed its concern regarding t he practice followed by BIS for 
issuing certification.   BIS has started a simplified procedure for granting  licenses to industry 
which may put all checks and balances of normal pro cedure to naught. This simplified 
procedure, while it expedites the process of grant of license; it in the process violates many 
provisions of BIS Act/ Rules/ Regulations.  The Committee, recommends that necessary action 
should  be taken by BIS to correct the procedure so  that it does not put companies applying 
for license under normal procedure to disadvantage.  
 
32. While BIS has set bench marks for its various a ctivities in its Citizens’ Charter, The 
Committee recommends that regular reviewing of the achievements of these bench marks 
should be done religiously so that the basic purpose of establishing BIS is not defeated.

2. While scrutinizing these Orders, the Committee noted in some cases
considerable time lag between issue of notifications and their laying. The
annexed statement also indicates the period of delay in cases where notifications
have not been laid as per the schedule prescribed by the Committee. The
Committee observed that out of total 321 delayed notifications there were 185
notifications where no delay statement was appended. However, the bulk of
delayed notifications were from Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
which cames around 79.75% of total delayed notifications.
The observations/recommendations of the Committee in respect of the
specific Ministries/Departments where delay in laying of Notifications has been
noticed are as follows: -
(i) Ministry of Agriculture
(Department of Agriculture and Cooperation and Department of Animal
Husbandry Dairying and Fisheries)
Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agriculture and Cooperation)
have laid 18 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 1 to 18) out of which 2 notifications (Sl.
Nos. 1 and 16) have been delayed by 3 and 9 months respectively. There was
no delay statement attached with one notification (Sl. No. 1) which was delayed
by 3 months. Another notification (Sl. No. 16) was delayed by 9 months but
Ministry has appended delay statement indicating the reason of the delay.
Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Animal Husbandry Dairying and
Fisheries) have laid 4 notifications (Sl. Nos. 19 to 22) All of these were delayed
by 5 months to 46 months and accompanied with delay statements. The reasons
of delay given therein are as under:-
“As per consolidated guidelines of framing/amendment/relaxation of
Recruitment Rules issued by DoPT OM No. AB.14017/48/2010-
Estt.(RR) dated 31.12.2010, para 5.3 of Part-V stipulates that “Although
the Recruitment Rules are statutory in nature, the copies of the notification
of the same need not be placed on the Table of both the Houses of

6
Parliament as Article 309 of the Constitution, under which these are
framed, does not prescribe this being done”. The Coconut Development
Board (Group ‘C’ post) Recruitment Regulations, 2012 have been framed
as per above mentioned guidelines of DoPT. Hence, it was not laid on
the Table of both the Houses of Parliament. The delay may kindly be
condoned.”
The Committee is unable to accept the reason given by the Ministry
for delay in laying of notifications despite the recommendations of the
Committee in this regard in its 82nd Report (para 4.31) which clearly
says that “... There is no reason why the Rules made under Article 309 of
the Constitution should not be laid before Parliament. There have been
some cases where the Rules made under Article 309 of the Constitution have
been laid before the Parliament. The Committee, therefore, strongly feels
and recommends that in order to maintain a uniform practice all the rules
made under delegated authority whether under various act of Parliament or
Article 309 of the Constitution should be laid before the Parliament. In
case, however, Government feels that the non-existence of the laying provision
in Article 309 is the reason for not laying the Rules made thereunder, the
Committee recommends that Article 309 of the Constitution be suitably
amended, so as to ensure that all the Rules made thereunder are laid before
the Parliament.” The Committee also takes note of the inordinate delay
of approximately 46 months in laying Rules which is not just acceptable
to the Committee and it recommends that Ministry of Agriculture should
in future strictly adhere to the laying procedure and whenever a delay
occurs, the Parliament is kept informed of the reason for the same by
appending a delay statement. The Committee hopes that Ministry would
strive to lay the notifications on the Table of the House at the first earliest
opportunity available.
(ii) Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers
(Department of Pharmaceuticals)
Only one notification that the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers

7
(Department of Pharmaceuticals) (Sl. No. 23) have laid was delayed by 5
months and no delay statement appended thereto. The Committee is not
happy over the delay in laying of the only notification by the Ministry of
Chemicals and Fertilizers (Department of Pharmaceuticals) by 5 months.
Further there is no delay statement appended to that giving reason as to
what caused such delay. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the
Ministry to take care that such instances of delay do not recur in future
and in case of any delay in laying, a delay statement should invariably be
appended.
(iii) Ministry of Civil Aviation
Ministry of Civil Aviation have laid only three Notifications (Sl. Nos. 24
to 26) on the Table of the House during the Session. There has been delay of 7
months each in case of Sl. No. 24 and 25 and delay of 6 months in case of Sl.
No. 26. The Ministry has attached delay statement with each of these delayed
notifications and cited administrative reasons for not laying the notifications in
time.
The Committee hopes that the Ministry would avoid such instances
of delay in laying of subordinate legislation in future and would remove
lacuna, if any, administrative or any other causing delay. The Committee
also impresses upon the Ministry to take note of the fact that in case
there is a delay in the laying of any Statutory Notifications, the same
should be accompanied by a delay statement while it is being laid . The
Committee also advises the Ministry of Civil Aviation to avoid recurrence
of delays due to administrative reasons in future.
(iv) Ministry of Communication and Information Technology
(Department of Information Technology and Department of Posts)
Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (Department
of Information Technology) have laid 2 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 37-38) and out
of these notification one was delayed by 6 months with no delay statement

8
attached to it. The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology
(Department of Posts) have laid only one Notification (Sl. No. 39) which was
delayed by 5 months. The Notification was attached with delay statement. The
reasons of delay given by the Ministry is as under:-
“The copies of the Gazette Notification which was published in the Gazette
of India Extraordinary, Part II – Section 3 – sub Section (i) vide No. 497
[GSR 734 (E)] dated October 01, 2012 regarding revision of Speed Post
tariff could not be laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha during the winter
Session of Parliament due to the paucity of time. The notification is now
being laid on the Table of Rajya Sabya during the Budget Session of
Parliament”
The Committee noted with serious concern that Ministry of
Communication and Information Technology (Department of
Information Technology and Department of Posts) have failed to lay the
notifications in time on the Table of the House due to paucity of time.
The laying of notifications on the Table of the House is a statutory
obligation which should be fulfilled without delay. However, the Ministry
have shown lukewarm approach towards their duty toward Parliament.
The Committee recommends that Ministry of Communication and
Information Technology should adhere strictly to the schedule as
recommended by the Committee in its 131
st Report for timely laying of
Subordinate Legislation. The Committee hope that Ministry would avoid
citing such unworthy reasons for delay in future.
(v) Ministry of Corporate Affairs
Ministry of Corporate Affairs have laid 20 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 51 to
70). Out of these 10 Notifications have been delayed by 3 to 5 months. Only
one delayed Notification (Sl. No. 52) was attached with delay statement and
other nine Notifications (Sl. Nos. 53 to 61) did not have any delay statement
citing the exact reasons for delay. The Ministry has stated the following reasons
of delay in regard to G.S.R. 736 (E):-

9
“The notification relating to the GSR No. 736 (E) dated 01.10.2012 on
Amendment in Rule 10(i) of Companies (Issue of Indian Depository
Receipt) Rules, 2004 was sent to Government Press for printing on
01.10.2012. The said notification could not be laid before both the Houses
of Parliament during winter session of the Parliament, 2012 due to delay
in receiving the Gazette copy of the notification by this Ministry and
when it was collected, the session was over on 19.12.2012 (Rajya Sabha)
and 20.12.2012 (Lok Sabha). Hence the said notification got delayed.”
The Committee regrets to note that Ministry of Corporate Affairs
have delayed laying of a number of notifications, many of which do not
have delay statement attached to them. The Committee invites attention
to its recommendations contained in its 135th Report that in case of
delay in laying of notifications, delay statement should invariably be
accompanied with them. As for reason of delay tendered by Ministry for
one notification (Sl. No. 52) stating that delay was caused due to late
receipt of printed copies of notifications, the Committee would like to
impress upon the Ministry of Corporate Affairs to evolve suitable
mechanism to eliminate such instances of delay in future particularly
on account of delay in receiving printed copies of the notifications. The
Committee further recommends that the Ministry should take note of
the time schedule as prescribed by it for laying of Subordinate Legislation
and take necessary corrective steps so that such instances do not recur.
(vi) Ministry of Defence
The Ministry of Defence have laid 4 Notifications and out of which two
were delayed by 3 to 8 months. One of the Notification had delay statement
attached to it whereas another did not have any delay statement with it. The
reasons for delay given by the Ministry are as under:-
“The Jalandhar Cantonment Octroi (Amendment) Bye-laws, 2012 were
issued on 12.06.2012 from the file of Jalandhar Cantonment Board under
the signature of its Chief Executive Officer (CEO). As such the File was

10
returned to Jalandhar Cantonment Board through DGDE on 13.06.2012,
but the published copy of the Notification could be received in the Ministry
only on 4.2.2013. As such, the Notification could not be laid during
Winter Session of Parliament, 2012.
The delay in laying of papers on the Table of Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha is
due to delay in getting published copies of the Notification. It is requested
that the marginal delay on the part of Ministry of Defence may kindly be
condoned.”
The Committee finds that laying of notifications was delayed due
to late receipt of printed copies of notifications in the Ministry. In this
context the Committee observes that it is Ministry’s responsibility to
ensure that Subordinate Legislation is laid before the Parliament within
the prescribed schedule and accordingly, it is for the Ministry only to
ensure that they receive the same timely from the statutory bodies under
them. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Defence may
take necessary remedial measures to ensure that papers are received
timely in the Ministry from the statutory bodies.
(vii) Ministry of Environment and Forests
Ministry of Environment and Forests have laid 5 Notifications (Sl. Nos.
75 to 79) during the Session. Out of these, three Notifications (Sl. Nos. 75 –
76 and 78) were delayed by 4 months to 6 months and moreover no delay
statement was appended to any of three delayed notifications.
The Committee notes that three of its notifications which were not
only delayed by four to six months also did not have any delay statement
attached to them. The Committee views it seriously and reiterate its
recommendations (contained in its 135th Report) that in case there is
delay in laying of Statutory Orders, the concerned Ministry/Department
should invariably append a delay statement. The Committee further
impresses the Ministry that it is their obligation towards the Parliament

11
to invariably apprise it about the reasons for delay through delay
statement in case they are unable to lay any Subordinate Legislation on
time.
(viii) Ministry of Finance
(Department of Financial Services)
Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) have laid 31
Notifications (Sl. Nos. 101 to 131). Out of these 9 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 111,
116 – 122 and 131) were delayed. The delay period ranges from 10 months to
31 months. The Ministry had attached delay statement with 8 notifications
whereas no statement was attached/appended with one notification. The reasons
for delay given by the Ministry is as under:-
“The Copies of the Gazettee Notifications could not be laid on the Table
of the Rajya Sabha as printed copies of the same were not received from
Regional Rural Banks in time. The delay has occurred as the Regional
Rural Banks which are spread out all over the country have to send the
Regulations to Government Press, New Delhi for publication. Thereafter,
these are sent back to the concerned Regional Rural Banks which then
sent it to the Ministry. The delay is thus in the administrative procedure/
process.”
The Committee does not accept the reasons of delay given by the
Ministry of Finance (Department of Financial Services) and expresses
its serious concern over such inordinate delay which ranges from 10
months to 31 months. The Committee wonders that how can
administrative procedural process take 10 to 31 months to receive
Notifications and complete procedural formalities. The Committee feels
that Ministry did not take adequate precaution to avoid the delay and
made no serious efforts to lay the Notifications in time which is in
contravention of its statutory obligation to Parliament. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry must take appropriate step to remove
lacuna, if any, administrative or any other, causing such long delay and

12
wish it would strive to keep delay to the minimum by playing a more
proactive role and pursuing concerned organisations to act with
promptness in future.
(ix) Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
(Department of Health and Department of AYUSH)
The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (Department of Health) have
laid 7 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 228 to 234). Only one Notification was delayed
by 8 months. However, no delay statement was enclosed with it.
Department of AYUSH have also laid 5 Notifications and one Notification
was delayed by 3 months and laid with delay statement attached to it. The
reasons given by the Ministry are as follows:-
“Laying of Gazette Notification of amendment made in Rule 161 of the
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 vide GSR No. 844 (E) dated 16.11.2012
regarding “insertion of botanical names of plants based ingredients along
with plant part(s) and form of ingredients to be mentioned on label”
published by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare was to be laid in
both Houses of Parliament. However due to the fact that in the final
notification some typographical error was observed and it had to be
rectified as per the prescribed procedure, hence, the notification could
not be laid within the stipulated time period. After rectification of the
error, now the notification is being submitted along with amended version
GSR No. 105 (E) dated 19.02.2013 before both the Houseds of Parliament.”
The Committee have noted the reason cited by the Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare that due to typographical error, the
notification could not be laid in time. The reasons given by the Ministry
seems to be justified and well taken. The Ministry should in future take
care that such instances do not recur and that notification were laid
within the time schedule prescribed by the Committee. The Committee,
therefore, impresses upon the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to

13
be watchful so that such error do not occur and consequential delay is
avoided in future. The Committee also emphasises that in case of delay
in laying of notifications, Ministry should append delay statement with
the notifications.
(x) Ministry of Home Affairs
The Ministry of Home Affairs have laid 21 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 240 -
260) during the Session. Out of total Notifications laid 14 Notifications have
been delayed. Out of these 12 Notifications have average delay period of 5
months whereas one Notification (Sl. No 240) was delayed by 4 months and
no delay statement was appended to 13 notifications. One Notification (Sl. No.
242) was delayed by 12 months and also had delay statement appended to it.
The reasons given by the Ministry are as follows:-
“Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Grant-in-Aid to Panchayati Raj Institutions)
(Amendment) Rules, 2012 was published in the Andaman & Nicobar
Gazette (Extraordinary) vide notification No. 08 dated 20/01/2012. As
per laid down procedure, the said Rules should have been laid as soon as
may be after it is made before each House of Parliament while it is in
session for a total period of 30 days. It could not be laid before both the
Houses of Parliament in time for want of certain clarifications from UT
of Andaman & Nicobar Administration. Clarifications sought from the
Andaman & Nicobar Administration have now been received.
The delay is regretted. These Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Grant-in-Aid
to Panchayati Raj Institutions) (Amendment) Rules, 2012 are now being
laid in both the Houses of Parliament in current session.”
The Committee expresses its unhappiness over the large proportion
of Notifications, which comes around 67% of total notifications, being
delayed by the Ministry. The Committee further takes serious note of
the fact that the Ministry in majority of cases did not even bother to
provide the reasons for such delayed laying of Notifications. In absence

14
of any delay statement with any of the delayed notifications, Committee
finds it difficult to ascertain causes of delay. The Committee invites
attention to the recommendations made in its 135th Report wherein it is
laid down that it is essential to append a delay statement in case of delay
in laying of statutory orders. The committee, therefore, impresses upon
the Ministry of Home Affairs to strictly adhere to the time schedule in
laying of Notifications and should invariably append delay statement in
each case of delayed notifications .
(xi) Ministry of Human Resource Development
(Department of Higher Education)
The Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of Higher
Education) have laid 7 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 261 to 267). Out of which 3
notifications were delayed by 4 to 5 months. All the delayed notifications were
appended with delay statement. The reasons given by the Ministry is that it
took some time to complete the procedural formalities and therefore, papers
could not be laid in time.
The Committee is not convinced of the vague reasons of delay
given by the Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of
Higher Education) that due to time taken to complete procedural
formalities, the Ministry could not lay the notifications in time. If, it
was so, the Ministry should have foreseen the things beforehand and
would have acted promptly. The Committee castigates this lackadaisical
approach by the Ministry and advises them to take care in future in
laying of notifications so that delay could be avoided.
(xii) Ministry of Law and Justice
(Department of Justice & Department of Legal Affairs)
Ministry of Law and Justice (Department of Justice) have laid one
Notification (Sl. No. 280) on the Table of the House with a delay period of one
year and five months without any delay statement appended to it. Department

15
of Legal Affairs have laid 4 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 281 to 284). All the 4
notifications were delayed and delay ranges from 8 months to 17 months.
However, all the Notifications laid by Department of Legal Affairs were appended
with delay statement. The reasons of delay given by the Department is that due
to voluminous work throughout the year, work relating to laying of notifications
could not be done in time inadvertently.
The Committee accepts that Ministry of Law and Justice is laden
with voluminous work and it may happen that the work may remain
undone inadvertently. However, the Committee impress upon the
Ministry that it is their statutory obligation to lay the notifications in
time on the Table of the House. Therefore Committee hopes that Ministry
would strive to adhere to laying schedule and avoid recurrence of such
delays in future.
(xiii) Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (Department
of Personnel and Training)
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions (Department of
Personnel and Training) have laid 10 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 285 to 294). Two
of these Notifications were delayed and the delay period was 5 months and 3
month each. The delay statement was appended with one of these Notifications.
The reasons of delay is given as under:-
“A copy of the Notification could be obtained only on 26.12.2012.
However, by the date the Winter Session of the Parliament was over.”
The Committee is not convinced of the reason given by the Ministry
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions that notification was
received on 26.12.2012 and by then Parliament’s winter Session was
already over. The Committee advises the Ministry of Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions to be more vigilant in future so that such delay
could be avoided.

16
(xiv) Ministry of Railways
Ministry of Railways have laid 4 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 298 to 301).
Only one of them (Sl. No. 300) was delayed by 3 months and accompanied
with delay statement. The reasons given by the Ministry for delay is as under:-
“The Indian Railways (Penalties for activities affecting cleanliness at
railway premises) Rules, 2012 G .S.R. 846 (E) published in the Gazette
of India Extraordinary Part-II Section 3 Sub-section-I could not be laid
down on the Table of the House due to an inadvertent oversight. The
same is therefore laid on the Table of the House.”
The Committee recommends that such instances should not be
repeated in future. Ministry of Railways must endeavour to lay the
notifications on the Table of House with upmost promptness.
(xv) Ministry of Road Transport and Highways
The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways have laid highest number
of notification during the Session which come around 374 Notifications (Sl.
Nos. 302-675). Out of these 256 Notifications have been delayed. The Ministry
did not append any delay statement with 105 delayed notifications (Sl. Nos.
306–310, 313–326, 334–347, 355–56, 358, 362–369, 401–403, 407–410, 413–
414. 416–431, 434–451, 455–458, 461–463, 465–468, 472–474, 476 & 478–
479). However, 151 delayed notifications were appended with delay statements.
The delay period ranges from 3 months to 19 months. The reason of delay
given by the Ministry is that it took some time to collect the papers and complete
the procedural formalities therefore, papers could not be laid in time on the
Table of both Houses of Parliament.
The Committee does not accept the reasons of the delay given by
the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways that it took some time to
collect the papers and complete the procedural formalities. The
Committee wonders how can it take one year to receive Notifications
and to complete procedural formalities. The Committee feels that Ministry

17
did not take adequate precaution to avoid the delay. The Committee
further takes a serious view of the fact that even after delay of one year
in certain case Ministry did not feel it necessary to append a delay
statement so as to apprise the Parliament of the reasons of delay in
laying of Notifications on the Table of the House. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should initiate urgent measures so as to
avoid delay in completing the procedural formalities so that such delay
can be eliminated.
(xvi) Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
(Department of Social Justice and Empowerment)
The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment (Department of Social
Justice and Empowerment) have laid only one Notifications (Sl. No. 676)
which was delayed by 22 months and moreover Ministry did not even bother
to append a delay statement citing the reasons for such extraordinary delay on
their part.
The Committee is not happy that the only notification that Ministry
of Social Justice and Empowerment have laid, has been extraordinary
delayed. Further, there is no reason given for this delay. This is in
contravention of Committee’s recommendation given in its 135 Report
that Notification which are delayed should invariably be accompanied by
delay statement. The Committee would like the Ministry of Social Justice
and Empowerment to take necessary steps to obviate such delay and in
case of delay in laying of Notifications, delay statement should invariably
be accompanied with them.
(xvii) Ministry of Urban Development
Ministry of Urban Development have laid one Notifications (Sl. No. 683)
during the Session which was delayed by 8 months. The reasons given by the
Ministry for delay is as under:-
“Copies of the Annual Report and Annual Accounts of Delhi Urban Art

18
Commission (DUAC) for the year 2011-12 and Delhi Urban Art Commission
(Secretary) Recruitment Rules, 2012 which were required to be laid on the
Table of Rajya Sabha in the Winter Session of 2012 were sent to Rajya Sabha
Secretariat on 17.12.2012. However, these were returned by the Secretariat
citing shortage of time. Therefore, the same are being laid on the Table of
Rajya Sabha during the Budget Session, 2013.
Delay caused in laying the above documents on the Table of the Rajya
Sabha is regretted.”
The Committee is not convinced with the reasons given by the
Ministry of Urban Development that notification could not be laid in
time due to curtailment of the Winter Session of 2012. Committee
impresses upon the Ministry of Urban Development to endeavour to lay
the notification at the first available opportunity on the Table of the
House so as to fulfill statutory obligation.
Before the commencement of each Session of Parliament Ministries
are informed about the dates of sitting of House and dates allotted to
each Ministries. In case of laying of notifications, Ministries are informed
to bring the notifications to Committee Section 3 working days before
the day/date of laying so that laying process can be completed. But the
Ministries do not adhere to the time schedule and bring the copies for
laying at the fag end of the Session. This causes a great inconvenience
to the Secretariat. The Ministry of Urban Development is advised to
stick to the time schedule to avoid such situation.
The Committee, time and again have emphasized that laying or
rules/regulations/orders is a statutory obligation and should be completed
on priority basis within specified time-frame. The Ministry of Urban
Development should understand the implication of such failures. However,
the Ministry of Urban Development has not complied with the
recommendations of the Committee in this regard. The Committee once

19
again emphasizes that Ministry of Urban Development should adhere to
the time schedule in laying of notifications as prescribed in Committee’s
131st Report.
3. Committee impresses upon all the Ministries/Departments to take
immediate steps to ensure timely and proper laying of subordinate legislation.
The Committee, accordingly, wishes to bring to the notice of all Ministries/
Departments of the Government of India, particularly, the defaulting ones, the
following recommendations, as contained in its 131st, 135th, 152nd , 192nd
and 201st Reports:
“Orders required to be laid before the House should be laid (i) if
the House is not in Session, during the Session immediately following
the date of publication of the Order in the Official Gazette and (ii) if the
House is in Session, on the date of the publication of the Order, during
its continuance and in case the time lag between the date of publication
and the date of the closing of the Session is less than 15 clear days,
before the expiry of the Session immediately following the said Session.
All the Ministries/Departments of Government of India should henceforth
comply with this schedule in the matter of laying of the Orders issued
under various Acts of Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.
(131st Report)
(Presented on 15 December 2000)
“The Committee has, time and again, emphasized that it is essential
that in case there is a delay in the laying of Statutory Orders, the
concerned Ministry/Department should invariably append a delay
statement along with the notifications being laid so as to apprise
Parliament of the causes of delay. The Committee desires all Ministries/
Departments to take a note of this, since the intension is that through
the process of formulation of a delay statement the Ministry is able to
introspect, identify bottlenecks and devise remedial measures”.
(135th Report)
(Presented on 27 July 2001)

20
“In the opinion of the Committee, every notification should be
assigned a distinctive number in order to give it a separate identity and
similarly, no notification should be published/laid which does not carry a
notification number. The Committee expects all Ministries/Departments
of Government of India to exercise caution in this regard. In case where
there are more than one notifications under a single file, the Ministries/
Departments should ensure that the file number on each notification
should be suitably distinguished from one another.”
(152nd Report)
(Presented on 26 August 2004)
“In addition to the concern expressed by the Committee over delay
in laying of Notifications on the Table of the House, the Committee also
express their deep concern over delay in framing of rules/regulations
under different Acts. The Committee in its 47th report presented to the
House on 14.9.1981 has recommended that the rule-making process should
be completed within a period of six months of the coming into force on
an Act. The Committee has further recommended that in case a Ministry
is not able to adhere to this time limit, it should seek extension of time
for completing the rule-making process. The recommendation of the
committee reads as follows:-
“The Committee feels that the rule-making process could well have
been completed within the time limit of six months which the
Committee has laid down for making of rules under an Act after coming
into force of that Act. Where however, a Ministry does not find it possible
to adhere to the time limit, they should inform the Committee of the
reasons why they cannot make rules within the time limit and seek
extension of time for completing the rule-making process.”
The Committee is constrained to take note of the fact that the
Ministries/Departments of Government of India are not complying with
the Committee’s recommendation to complete the process of framing of

21
subordinate legislation contemplated under various Acts of Parliament
within a period of six months. At the same time, the Committee also
does not receive requests for extension of time for completing the rule-
making process in terms of its recommendations as above from most of
the Ministries/Departments. The Committee takes a serious note of the
prevailing situation in which the Ministries/Departments are neither
able to complete the task of framing rules/regulations under different
Acts within the given six months’ period nor do they suo-motu approach
the Committee for seeking extension of time. The Committee further
notes that in order to ensure timely framing of rules/regulations it has
taken an initiative to monitor the progress of framing of subordinate
legislation in respect of all legislations brought about by different
Ministries/Departments of Government of India from the year 2003
onwards with a view to ensure that the framing of subordinate legislation
is not delayed. The Committee, however, finds that the responses from
the Ministries/Departments have not been prompt in this monitoring
exercise undertaken on behalf of the Committee.
In view of the above position, the Committee once again reiterates
its recommendation that the Ministries/Departments should ensure
putting in place subordinate legislation positively within a period of six
months of coming into force of the Act. The Committee further
recommends that in case the Ministry fails to meet with this deadline,
they should invariably approach the Committee for seeking extension
of time. The Committee further recommends that in cases where the
time limit of six months is not adhered to, they should, while laying
rules/regulations before the Parliament invariably lay a statement
explaining the reasons why the framing of rules/regulations was delayed
beyond six months so as to keep the Parliament apprised of the compliance
of the Parliament’s mandate conferred upon the Executive.”
(192nd Report)
(Presented on 26 August 2011)

22
Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are laid by different Ministries
on the Table of the House under various provisions of parent Acts passed
by Parliament. These Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are published
in the official Gazette before being laid on the Table of the House. Even
after they are laid, it is very difficult to get access to these notifications.
The Committee recommends that such Rules/Regulations/Orders, etc.
laid on the Table of the House should be invariably uploaded on the
websites of respective Ministries immediately on the same day when
they have been laid on the Table of the House, for information of
Members of Parliament and people at large for their easy access.
201st Report
(Presented on 14th December, 2012)
