February    19, 2014 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

Report  
on the  
Marble Development and Conservation Rules, 2002  
 
I BACKGROUND 
 
 
 Marble a ‘minor mineral’ as defined in clause (e) of Section 3 of Mines and 
Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 is used widely in buildings, monuments 
and sculptures. It is know for its pleasant colours , smooth and uniform texture, moderate 
hardness, amenability to be quarried into big block s, smooth & shiny polished surface 
and silky feel. Though the occurrence of Marble has  been reported from many States in 
the country, however, deposits of economic importan ce are localized in Rajasthan, 
Gujarat, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh and also in Madhya  Pradesh as per recent reports. 
Rajasthan has the distinction of having the best am ong Indian resources of good quality 
marble. As per available data on marble resources a bout 64% of total resources are in 
Rajasthan and 21% in Jammu & Kashmir. The remaining  resources are distributed 
mainly in Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Harya na, Uttarakhand and Sikkim in 
descending order. In terms of production Rajasthan alone accounts for 94% of the total 
output. Further, over the years the export of marble has also increased.  
 
2. The Marble Development & Conservation Rules (MDM R), 2002 were brought 
into effect for the purpose of conservation, system atic development and scientific mining 
of marble and to provide a uniform framework that w ould be applicable throughout the 
country. In the background to these Rules it was in formed that a Group on Marble 
Development (GMD) was constituted on 22.9.1999 unde r the overall guidance and 
supervision of Granite Development Council to addre ss the difficulties faced by the 
Marble industries.  The Group on Marble Development  (GMD) in its meeting held on 2 
nd  
February, 2000 decided to constitute a Sub-Group un der the Chairmanship of Controller 
General, Indian Bureau of Mines to examine the mech anization in marble quarries. The 
Sub-Committee recommended that Marble Development a nd Conservation Rules could 
be framed in line with the Granite Conservation and  Development Rule, 1999.   
Accordingly, in consultation with stakeholders, the  Marble Development and 
Conservation Rules ( Annexure-I) were notified vide G.S.R. 369 (E) dated 15.5.2002.  

 
II  SALIENT FEATURES OF THE MARBLE DEVELOPMENT AND 
CONSERVATION RULES,  2002  
 
3.  Salient Features of the Marble Development and Conservation Rules, 2002 are as 
follows: 
 
i)  The rules apply to prospecting and quarrying of mar ble and are framed 
under Section 18 of MMDR Act, 1957 read with Sectio ns 21 and 26 for 
conservation and systematic development, scientific  mining of marble in 
the country and to provide a uniform framework in this regard. 
ii)  The rules make it mandatory to carry out prospectin g operations before a 
mining lease can be granted. 
iii)  The period of prospecting license shall not exceed two 
years. 
iv)  The period of mining lease shall not be less than t wenty years and shall 
not exceed thirty years. 
v)        Minimum area to be granted under lease sh all not be less than four 
hectares and not    
           more than fifty hectares, with the restr iction that any side of the area shall 
not be less              .         than 200 metres 
vi)  Preparation of a scheme of prospecting and prospect ing operations to be 
carried out in accordance with the said scheme is mandatory. 
vii)     The prospecting license holder for marble has to  submit a scheme of 
prospecting indicating the manner in which he propo ses to carry out the 
prospecting to the State Government within 60 days from the date of 
execution of prospecting license. Every holder of a  prospecting license for 
marble shall submit an annual report to the State Government. 
viii)  The rules provide for priority claim over a mining lease to the holder of a 
prospecting license if licensee applies for the min ing lease at thirty days 
before expiry of prospecting license. 
ix)  The Mining Plan duly approved shall be valid for the duration of the lease. 
x)  The rules provide for optimum deployment of certain  mining machinery 
to ensure production with minimum waste generation. 

xi)  On receipt of the application for grant of mining lease, the State Govt. shall 
take decision to grant precise area for said purpose. 
xii)  On receipt of communication about precise area the applicant shall submit 
a mining plan prepared by a recognized person. The Mining Plan 
submitted shall be approved by State Govt. on recei pt of the approved 
mining plan. The State Govt. will take a decision to grant the lease. 
xiii)  With a view to systematic and scientific mining, th e rules provide for 
removal and utilization of top soil, storage of ove rburden, waste rock, 
reclamation and rehabilitation of lands, precaution against air, water, noise 
pollution, restoration of flora, etc. 
xiv)  Employment of a mining engineer for carrying out pr ospecting and 
mining operations has been made mandatory. 
xv)  Submission of half-yearly and annual production ret urns has been 
provided for in the rules. 
xvi)  The provisions of the rules are also applicable to the government or its 
agencies carrying out mining operations. 
xvii)  The provisions of the Minor Mineral Concession Rule s framed by the 
respective State Governments under Section 15 of th e MMDR Act are 
applicable to the marble quarry leases to the exten t they are not repugnant 
with or inconsistent with the rules. 
 
III EXAMINATION OF RULES, OBSERVATIONS AND 
RECOMMENDATIONS  
 
4. Taking into consideration the importance of thes e Rules, the Committee took up 
for examination the Marble Development & Conservati on Rules (MDMR), 2002 and a 
questionnaire on the subject was forwarded to the M inistry of Mines for their comments/ 
clarifications on the 24 
th  January, 2003.  The Ministry furnished their 
comments/clarifications on the 19 th  September, 2003 (Annexure II) . A brief summary of 
the points raised by the Committee and the comments  of the Ministry are elaborated in 
the succeeding paragraphs along with the observatio ns/ recommendations of the 
Committee. 
 

5. The Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation ) Act, 1957 was enacted in 
1957, but the Marble Development and Conservation R ules, 2002 were framed and 
notified in the year 2002.   The Committee, accordi ngly, sought to know the manner in 
which the areas covered by these rule were being regulated in the absence of these rules.   
 
5.1 The Ministry informed the Committee that Marble  is a building stone which is a 
notified minor minerals under Section 3(e) of Mines  and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDRA Act). Section 15 of the MMDR Act empowers the State 
Governments to make rules in respect of minor minerals for regulating the grant of quarry 
lease, mining leases, or other concessions and for purposes connected therewith. 
Therefore, every State Government is competent to m ake rules in respect of marble 
resources in the State.     The grant of concession s in respect of minor minerals including 
building stones like marble, granite, etc. are gove rned by the Minor Mineral Concession 
Rules of the respective State Governments. While Se ction 15 of the  MMDR Act, 1957 
has denuded  the Central Government of powers to fr ame rules for regulating the grant of 
quarry lease, mining leases, or other concessions a nd for purposes connected therewith in 
respect of minor minerals, under section 18 of the MMDR Act, 1957, a duty has been 
cast upon the Central Government to take all steps to ensure systematic and scientific 
mining of all minerals, including minor minerals. 
5.2 The Ministry further informed that the Mineral Conservation and Development 
Rules, 1988, supplement the Mineral Concession Rule s, 1960 in ensuring systematic 
conservation and development of major minerals and are not applicable to minor 
minerals.  In view of the rising importance of marb le as an important mineral with 
sizeable export market, the Central Government felt  a need to notify Marble 
Development and Conservation Rules, 2002 separately , carefully delineating the areas 
delegated to the States under powers bestowed to th em under Section 15 of the MMDR 
Act, 1957, in the interest of uniform legislation a cross States for this important minor 
mineral.  Prior to enactment of the Marble Developm ent and Conservation Rules, 2002, 
there was no uniform statutory framework across the  States for systematic conservation 
and development of marble resources in the country.  The State Governments are 
responsible in all matters regarding minor minerals . Therefore, the State Governments, 

who, under their own State rules, had been regulati ng the areas now covered by the 
Marble Development and Conservation Rules, 2002, ha ve been made the administering 
authority for enforcing the Central rule as well. 
 
6. Rule 3(1)(o) Definition 
"Recognized person" means a qualified person grante d recognition by the 
competent authority under these rules to prepare mining plan.  
 
6.1 The Committee enquired as to who was the compet ent authority referred to in the 
Rules and whether there was any objection in defining the same in the Rule.   
 
6.2 The Ministry stated that the Competent Authorit y referred in rule 3(1) (o) is the 
State Government or any person authorized by the St ate Government. The competent 
authority would be different for different states d epending upon the State Government 
set up. In order to provide the flexibility to the State Government in deciding the 
competent authority in enforcing the various provis ions of the rules, the term has not 
been defined separately in the rules. The Mineral c oncession Rules, 1960, which is 
applicable for major minerals is also framed similarly.  
 
6.3  The Committee after considering the contentions of the Ministry is of the 
opinion that the Ministry should ensure that the ba sic qualifications of the 
Recognized person under Rule 3(1)(o) should be unif orm in all the States where 
substantial amount of Marble is found. This was ess ential to maintain a certain 
basic level of uniformity in the implementation of the Rules in different States and 
setting the standards’ of the basic qualifications for the Recognized person was one 
of them. 
 
7. Rule 5: Period for which prospecting license may be granted. 
 
 "The period for which a prospecting license may be granted shall not 'exceed two 
years". 

 
7.1 The Committee was apprehensive whether two year s period was sufficient for 
prospecting and whether the rules should not take c are for circumstances where more 
period is required for genuine reasons.   
 
7.2 Allaying the apprehensions of the Committee, th e Ministry informed that in all 
cases of exploring and prospecting for minerals, a finite period is prescribed in the 
interest of mineral development. Even in case of ma jor minerals, a reconnaissance 
permit, which interalia  involves aerial exploration, is granted only for a  fixed period of 
three years.   
7.3 As per the Marble Development & Conservation Ru les (MDMR), 2002, evidence 
of prospecting or establishing existence of marble has been made a prerequisite for the 
grant of mining/ quarry lease in a particular area.  The Government held extensive 
discussions with the marble mining industry and the  State Governments before deciding 
on the period for prospecting. It was the consensus  that a two-year period is sufficient to 
locate the marble deposits as these occur mostly as  surface deposits, and accordingly the 
rules have provided for the same. Granite Conservat ion and Development Rules, 1999 
(GCDR) also prescribe the same period for prospecti ng for granite, on similar 
considerations.   
 
7.4 The Committee noted the reply of the Ministry.    
 
8. Rule 7: Minimum and maximum area for grant of a mining lease . 
 
“Provided that the State Government, if it is satis fied on the basis of proposed 
production level, geological, topographical or othe r conditions, may for the 
reasons to be recorded in writing, grant a lease ov er an area more than the 
maximum area or less than the minimum area specified under this rule." 
 
8.1 The Committee felt that the rule seems to vest enormous discretion with the State 
Government in deciding the area of land for mining lease. Recording the reasons in 

writing is the only check envisaged in the rules to  prevent misuse of the discretion. Does 
government not contemplate any further safeguards i n this regard like prescribing a 
maximum limit that could not be crossed under any c ircumstances, or some other such 
conditions.   
 
8.2 The Ministry informed that the Marble Developme nt and Conservation Rules, 
2002, envisage that State Governments would be the administering authority for 
enforcing the same.  The State Governments are empo wered vide Section 15 of the 
MMDR Act, 1957 to make rules for grant of leases/co ncessions for minor minerals 
including for marble.  Though the Marble Developmen t and Conservation Rules, 2002, 
have prescribed minimum and maximum area that can b e granted under mining lease for 
marble, but under the administering authority of th is Central Rule, a duty has been cast 
upon the State Governments to use the discretion fo r deviation from the ceilings 
prescribed only in genuine circumstances while gran ting mining leases for this minor 
mineral, on the basis of production level, geological, topographic or other conditions.   
8.3 The Ministry further informed that a similar di scretion is available to the Central 
Government for relaxing the maximum area that can b e granted under a mining lease in 
the interest of mineral development for major miner als under Mineral Concession Rules, 
1960. Most of the important mineral based industria l concerns, including Central and 
State Public Sector Undertakings have been granted large mining leases in judicious 
exercise of the discretion. Therefore, prescribing a maximum limit that could not be 
crossed under any circumstances in case of granting  of mining lease for marble, a minor 
mineral, which is otherwise totally under jurisdict ion of the State Governments, perhaps 
cannot be justified in the federal structure. 
 
8.4 The Committee notes the comments/clarifications  offered by the Ministry is 
of the opinion that since the said Rules have been in effect for over a decade, the 
Government must have gained sufficient experience i n the working of these Rules. 
Therefore, the Ministry based on its experience sho uld come up with an advisory 
regarding the grounds on which relaxation may be gr anted under the Rules. Views 
of the concerned States may also be solicited in th is regard keeping in view the fact 

that the State Governments also have a major role i n deciding the area of land for 
granting of mining lease. Such an advisory would help expedite the process of taking 
decisions regarding relaxation of Rules concerning area requirements.  
 
9. Rule 9: Modification of Scheme of Prospecting  :- 
 
“(1)   A prospecting scheme prepared and submitted under rule 8 may be 
modified at any time on geological considerations b y the holder of a 
prospecting license during continuance of the prospecting license.   
 
(2) Any modification carried out under Sub-rule (1)  shall be intimated to the 
State Government or any person authorized in this b ehalf by that 
Government, by the holder of a prospecting licence within a period of 
fifteen days.” 
 
9.1 The Committee wanted a clarification as to the modification suggested by the 
holder of the prospecting licence need any formal a pproval by any body, what is the date 
from which the period of 15 days is to reckon, and what checks are there in the rule to 
ensure that the limitation of 15 days is not violated.   
 
9.2 The Ministry informed that the modification car ried out in the Prospecting 
Scheme submitted under rule 8(1) is only to be inti mated to the State Government or any 
person authorized in this behalf by that Government  within a period of 15 days from the 
date of such modification and no formal approval is  required. If a violation of this rule is 
detected, the holder of the Prospecting Licence is liable to punishment provided under 
Rule 41.  
 
9.3  The Committee while accepting the comments offered by the Ministry is of 
the opinion that some safeguards are needed to be p ut in place for the modifications 
in the prospecting scheme. Therefore, the intimatio n of modification submitted to 
the State Government or any other person authorized  in this behalf should be 
accompanied by a statement indicating the reasons f or making the modifications 
along with its financial and ecological implications. The Committee, therefore, urges 
the Ministry to amend the rules accordingly.   
 

10 Rule 12: Mining Plan as a pre-requisite to the grant of lease:  
  
2(a) For the renewal of any lease over an area exce eding one hectare the State 
Government shall require the lessee to submit a min ing plan duly 
approved by the State Government or any person auth orized in this behalf 
by that Government for the development of marble de posit in the area 
concerned. 
 
(b) For the purpose of renewal of a mining lease up to an area of one hectare, 
the State Government shall specify a simplified sch eme of mining to be 
submitted by the lessee for approval by the state G overnment or any other 
person authorized in this behalf. 
 
10.1 The Committee sought clarification as to wheth er the restriction of minimum area 
of four hectares provided in rule 7(1) for grant of  lease was also applicable in case of 
renewal of lease under the provisions of rule 12(2)  (a) & (b).  Also, how rule 12(2) is 
mentioning about one hectare of area.  
 
10.2  In response the Ministry stated that the Marb le Development and Conservation 
Rules 2002 have drawn a distinction between initial  grant of a mining lease and renewal 
of an existing mining lease.  Rule 7(1) and (2) pre scribe the minimum area and the 
maximum area that may be granted under a mining lea se.  Rule 12(1) states that no lease 
shall be granted unless there is an approved mining  plan.   This Rule complements Rule 
7(1) and (2) regarding grant of a mining lease.   W hile Rule 12(2)(a) provides that for 
renewal of any mining lease for an area of 1 hectar e and above, a mining plan should be 
submitted where as Rule 12(2)(b) provides that for smaller areas a simple scheme of 
mining should be submitted for approval of State Govement. 
10.3 Drawing a distinction between grant of a minin g lease and renewal of mining 
lease in so far as minimum size of the lease is con cerned and submission of mining plans 
in the Marble Development and Conservation Rules, 2 002 has a background.  Marble 
quarries have existed for last few centuries in are as like Makrana in Rajasthan, and with 
time, inheritance rights over small fragmented quar ries have come into existence, which 
cannot be suddenly reversed.  Before framing of Mar ble Development and Conservation 
Rules, 2002 the States had already granted smaller mining/quarry leases for marble and 
such areas are already broken.  The Central rules i ntend to provide for scientific and 

systematic mining for fresh mining leases for marbl e, in virgin areas. Hence the 
restriction of minimum area of 4 hectares provided under rule 7(1) for grant of lease is 
not applicable in case of renewal of such existing quarry leases of less then the minimum 
prescribed area. Rule 12(2), therefore, provides for scheme of mining for such areas up to 
one hectare in extent, as and when they come up for renewal.   
10.4 The Committee noted the reply of the Ministry  
 
11. Rule 15-Approval and submission of mining plan . 
 
 “On receipt of the application for grant of mining  lease for undertaking mining 
operations for marble, the State Government shall t ake decision to grant precise area for 
the said purpose and communicate such decision to t he applicant and on receipt of the 
communication from the State Government of the prec ise area to be granted, the 
applicant shall submit a mining plan within a perio d of three months from the date on 
which such communication is received or such other period as may be allowed by the 
State Government for approval and the said mining p lan shall incorporate :-
………………” 
 
 
11.1 The Committee was of the view that Rule 15 gav e discretionary powers to the 
State Governments for submitting by the applicant t he mining plan for approval. It 
therefore sought clarification as to whether the ru les should not be uniform for all and 
leave no scope for different application and whethe r Government had any objection in 
prescribing certain checks to ensure that submissio n of mining plans was not unduly 
delayed. 
 
11.2  In response the Ministry submitted that while  applying for a mining lease, the 
applicant cannot submit the mining plan, because he is not aware of how much and which 
part of the area may ultimately be granted to him.  Rule 15 therefore provides that he has 
to submit the mining plan only after the State Gove rnment has taken a decision to grant 
him a lease over a precise area.   Therefore, the a pplicant is given three months time or 
such other period as may be allowed to submit the m ining plan for the precise area 
incorporating nature and extent of the marble depos it,  details of geology and lithology, 
extent of manual mining, mining by the use of machi nery, etc.  over which the State 
Government has taken a decision to grant him the le ase.  Preparation of the mining plan 

is time consuming and the minimum period of 3 month s given by the State Government 
is reasonable.  An applicant, cannot be granted a n ew mining lease unless he submits the 
plan and the State Government approves it.  The sub mission of mining plans within time 
is always in the interest of applicant himself.  In case of undue delay not acceptable to the 
State Government, the Government has powers to revo ke the decision to grant the said 
lease under the State Minor Mineral Concession Rules. 
 
11.3  The Committee while acknowledging the content ions of the Ministry 
is of the opinion that  the Ministry should make ef forts to use the latest electronic 
networks for expediting the process of submission o f mining plans. The Ministry 
should make efforts to motivate the State Governments to move towards a paperless 
procedure by setting up websites for submission of applications and mining plans. 
This would also help the process of monitoring of s ubmission of documents in a time 
bound manner.  
 
12. Rule 16(4) -  Mining plan as a pre-requisite to the commencement of mining 
operations : 
 
“The State Government or any person authorized in t his behalf by that 
Government may approve the modifications under sub- rule(3) or approve with 
such alterations as it may consider expedient.” 
 
12.1 The Committee wanted to know whether the Gover nment had any objection in 
providing for recording in writing the reasons for making alterations or modifications in

12.2 The Ministry accepted the views of the Committ ee and stated that the State

Committee.

“ If approval or refusal of the scheme of mining is  not conveyed to the holder of

13.1 The Committee felt that the words ‘whenever co mmunicated’ were vague and

submission of applications and documents. Such a ne twork, if put in place, would 
ensure better monitoring and transparency. The Comm ittee, therefore, urges the

“Every holder of a prospecting licence or a lease s hall take all possible 
precautions for the protection of environment and c ontrol of pollution while 

conducting prospecting,  mining or processing of ma rble in the area for which 
such licence or lease is granted”.

norm existing in this regard and, it not, how matte rs of details are being enforced in the

Mines should take the initiative in coordination with the Ministry of Environment & 
Forest for getting the necessary subordinate legisl ation framed with particular 
reference to marble and related operations. It, the refore, urges the Ministry to take 
necessary steps in this regard.

15.3 The Committee noted the reply of the Ministry.

“Every leaseholder shall undertake in a phased mann er restoration, reclamation

I  BACKGROUND 
The Committee received a representation from the In dian Railway Loco Runningmen 
Organization (IRLRO) on the issue of  hours of working of loco running staff in Indian Railways 
on 26 
th  September, 2011.  The representation was forwarded  to the Ministry of Railways and the 
Ministry of Labour & Employment for their comments/  clarifications.  The Ministry of Railways 
furnished their comments/ clarifications on the 4 h November, 2011 (Annexure-I)  which was 
duly forwarded to IRLRO on 21 st  November, 2011.   The Ministry of Labour & Employm ent 
also furnished their comments on the representation  of IRLRO on 12 th  November, 2012 
(Annexure-II). This was also forwarded to IRLRO on 20 th  November, 2012.  In the meantime, 
IRLRO in August, 2012 submitted a rejoinder on the reply of the Ministry of Railways which 
was again forwarded to that Ministry for their comm ents/ clarifications in September, 2012. The 
Ministry of Railways again furnished their comments /clarifications on the rejoinder on 28 th  
September, 2012 (Annexure-III). This was also forwarded to IRLRO on 11 th  October, 2012.   
The Committee also heard the representatives of IRL RO, the Ministry of Railways and Ministry 
of Labour & Employment on the subject on 4 th  October, 2013.  Minutes of the meeting are 
enclosed at Annexure-IV . 
 
II EXAMINATION OF RULES AND OBSERVATIONS/  RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
2. The issues raised by IRLRO and the comments/ cla rifications of the Ministry of Railways 
and the Ministry of labour & Employment received th ereon were examined at length by the 
Committee.  Section 130 under Chapterof the Railway s Act, 1989 contains provisions for 
‘Regulation of Hours of Work and Period of Stay.’  The entire Chapter XIV of the Railways Act 
covers this issue.  Section 132 of the Act ‘Limitat ion of Hours of Work’ is more specific while 
Section 136 of the Act provides for powers to make rules.   Preliminary examination of these 
Rules suggested that the Ministry of Labour are an important stakeholder on this issue.  The 
Committee, therefore, decided that for harmonious i nterpretation and application of these Rules, 
it was important to hear both the Ministry of Railw ays and the Ministry of Labour & 

Employment on the issue.  The Committee, accordingl y, held discussions on the subject matter 
with the representatives of IRLRO, Ministry of Rail ways and the Ministry of Labour & 
Employment on the 4 th  October, 2013.   
 
III DISCUSSION WITH  IRLRO     
 
3. During the course of discussion, IRLRO submitted  before the Committee that the first 
item and first subject allotted to the Ministry of Labour in the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 
is the “Hours of Employment of the Railway Employee s (HOER), other than Factory Act.”  In 
1946 and again in 1969, it was the Labour Ministry which appointed the Chairman/ Labour 
Tribunal, respectively, on the issue of duty hours of railway employees including Loco Running 
men.   Chief Labour Commissioner- Central (CLC(C ))  Ministry of Labour has declared itself as 
Authority on Hours of Employment on the Ministry of  Labour’s  website.  Also, the Regional 
Labour Commissioner- Chennai (RLC (C )), Chennai ha s categorically declared itself as 
Appellate Authority on HOER-2005 for classifications.   
 
4. In IRLRO’s opinion, the High Power Committee ann ounced by the Ministry of Railways 
consisting of Ex-Secretary of the Ministry of Food Processing Industry as Chairman and three 
retired Railway officials as Members is contrary to  policy decision taken in the NC/JCM (JCA).   
The Administrative Committee constituted by Railway  Board on the 25 
th  May, 2011 is totally 
against the said Agreement notified by DOPT.   
 
5. On being enquired by the Committee about their e xact grievance and the redressal they 
wanted, IRLRO submitted that they were not getting weekly compulsory rest as per the ILO 
C001 Convention of 1919.   IRLRO listed out their g rievances as follows: (i) No fixed upper 
limit of Duty Hours; (ii) No compulsory weekly rest  at present; (iii) No Break during duty hours 
for having food, refreshments and attending to natu re’s call; and (iv) No upper limit for night 
duties in a month/ week at present.   IRLRO requested for the following possible solutions: (i) To 
fix upper limit of Duty Hours to maximum of eight h ours per day normally; (ii) To fix 
compulsory weekly rest by devising a suitable mechanism for all drivers; (iii) To issue directions 
for defined and compulsory Break of half an hour ev ery five hours during normal working; and 

(iv) To issue directions for defined and compulsory  limit of 2-3 nights continuous working and 
maximum ten nights in a month.    
 
6. The Committee notes that IRLRO is not recognized by  Railway Board.  However, 
they are registered with the Ministry of Labour und er the category of Trade Union and 
represent around 7000 employees including drivers a nd assistants.   At the same time 
Committee feels  it cannot turn its back to the genuine grievances o f the loco running staff 
in the Indian Railways and has decided to take a ch aritable view in the matter.  The 
Committee observes that out of a total sanctioned s trength of around 88,000 posts for 
drivers in Indian Railways, 20% of posts were lying vacant .   
 
IV DISCUSSION WITH THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS  
 
7. The Ministry of Railways in their submission bef ore the Committee clarified that the 
decision to constitute the High Power Committee had  been taken by the Ministry of Railways, 
Railway Board keeping in view the minutes of the NC / JCM with the approval of full Board and 
Hon’ble Minister of Railways in consultation with t he recognized Railway Labour Federations.  
Railway Ministry is the competent authority in all matters of rail transport, especially in regard to 
Regulation of the Hours of Work & Period of Rest of  railway employees in terms of Chapter 
XIV of the Railways Act, 1989.  As per Rule 4 of th e Railway Servants (Hours of Work & 
Period of Rest) Rules, 2005, the appeals against th e classification of railway servants are 
preferred with the Appellate Authority, the Ministr y of Labour & Employment.  Decisions 
delivered by Regional labour Commissions (RLCs) are not final. Any railway servant or Railway 
Administration aggrieved by a decision of RLC may p refer an appeal with the Appellate 
Authority, i.e. the Ministry of Labour & Employment .  Working hours of running staff are 
regulated in accordance with the provisions contained in the Railways Act, 1989 and the Railway 
Servants (Hours of Work & Period of Rest) Rules, 20 05 have been framed with the approval of 
the Ministry of Labour & Employment.   
 
8. The Committee observed that there was not a singl e representative from the Labour 
Ministry in the High Powered Committee appointed by  the Railway Ministry.  In Committee’s 
view, Labour Ministry is the nodal Ministry to impl ement the labour legislations in the 

country not only for the Railways, but also for the  entire country.  The Committee failed to 
understand, that when under their own initiative, t he Railway Ministry were convinced 
that the workers are really having certain grievanc es regarding their working conditions, 
lunch/ break time, maintaining of the rail time-tab le, etc., what prevented them from 
taking a  pro-active action and avoiding this kind of unrest.  The Committee failed to 
understand why Railway Ministry did not take pro ac tive action rather than going for 
appeal or law.   In Committee’s view, Railways should not accept ill egitimate demands at 
the cost of the efficiency of the Railways and inco nvenience of passengers, but, this should 
not prevent them from taking a pro-active stand and  solving their problems at their own 
level.   
  
9. Railway Board informed that when the High Power Committee was appointed, need was 
not felt to call people from outside.  Railways was  in a position to carry out a lot of things 
required to be done and need was not felt to seek c ooperation/ consultation with   other 
Ministries.  Railway Board stated that based on the recommendations of the Committee, Railway 
Ministry would hold consultations with other Ministries.  Regarding pro-active role, the Ministry  
stated that each driver was given a specific train link based on the train time-table schedule with 
his approval.   Regarding shortage of drivers, the Committee was informed that 25% of drivers 
were kept on reserve by way of leave or rest-giving  period.  In this sense, there was shortage of 
18% in the over all ‘safety category’ and shortage for loco pilots was less than this.  104 duty 
hours was the upper limit and it did not cross the average of 91-92 duty hours.  In case of railway 
accidents, the Commissioner of Railway Safety appoi nted to look into the matter first checked 
whether the limit of hours of duty of the driver ha d not been crossed and whether he had been 
given proper rest.   
 
10. The Committee, however, expressed distress over the  lack of sensitivity showed by 
the Railway Ministry towards their loco drivers.  I n the Committee view, public perception 
was, while drivers are over fatigued, they are also  human beings.  The Committee 
expressed anguish that the Ministry of Railways had  come before the Committee 
unprepared on the issue at hand and did not even ha ve information on the number of loco 
driver posts vacant at present.   The Committee des ired to take a charitable view in the 

matter taking into account the efficiency of Railwa ys.  Loco runners and signal staff are 
very important for the railways.  Keeping in view t he grave situations under which they 
have to work and the fatigue and mental stress/ strain that the Loco Running Staff undergo 
while on duty- which have a direct affect on their health –these are problems that have to 
be reviewed periodically to lessen the physical and  mental stress that they are put to.  The 
Committee impresses upon the Railways and expects t hem to take a pro-active stand and 
solve the problems at their own level.   The Committee disapproves the Railway Ministry’s 
lethargy in responding to the genuine grievances of  its staff and expects the Ministry will 
come out with possible solutions to these grievances.      
 
V DISCUSSION WITH THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR & EMPLOYME NT   
 
11. The Ministry of Labour & Employment in their su bmission before the Committee stated 
that in terms of Sections 135, 7 and 9 of the Railw ays Act, 1989 and Rules 3, 5 and 14 of the 
Railways Servants (Hours of Work and Period of Rest ) Rules, 2005, officers of the Ministry of 
Labour & Employment are bestowed with certain power s and duties, and, quoted from the 
Allocation of Work Rules, 1961 which states that in  respect of Union Railways- Payment of 
Wages, Trade Disputes and Hours of Work for Employe es- these subjects come under the 
Ministry of Labour.  The 1961 Rules clearly mention  that “Government means the Central 
Government in the Ministry of Labour and Employment ”.  Not only in Railways, but also in 
mines, steel and power, working conditions of labou r and hours of work was governed by 
Labour Ministry.  In case of appeal, dispute goes t o Labour Ministry which takes the final 
decision.  Railways only have right to implement th e recommendations.  Also, in case of 
amendment to the rules, Labour Ministry is to be consulted.    
 
12. In the opinion of the Ministry of Labour & Empl oyment, the Chief Labour Commissioner 
(Central) who is heading the Central Industrial Relations Machinery (CIRM) who are responsible 
for maintaining harmonious relations between the Ma nagement and Unions should also be 
associated as a Member of the Committee.  The Ministry further suggested inclusion of a suitable 
representative from Ministry of Health for proper s tudy of fatigue and mental stress/strain 
undergone by the loco running staff. To have a broa d-based consultation on tri-partite basis, the 
Ministry also recommended having representatives of  the recognized Railway 

Unions/Federations in the High Power Committee to f acilitate meaningful examination of issues 
which would, in the long run, ensure harmonious industrial relations in the Railways.  
 
VI ANALYSIS / OBSERVATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS   
 
13. The Committee observes that pursuant to the pro visions of Section 136 of the 
Railways Act, 1989, Ministry of Railways in consult ation with Ministry of Labour  framed 
the ‘Railways Servants (Hours of work & Period of R est) Rules, 2005.  The Ministry of 
Railway has contented that fixing of duty hours as per the Act and Rules framed 
thereunder comes within their jurisdiction.  Howeve r, when these Rules were framed, 
Ministry of Labour was also consulted.  Thus, in Co mmittee’s view Ministry of Labour is 
also a stakeholder.  Also, in the ‘Railways Servant s (Hours of Work & Period of Rest) 
Rules, 2005’, Ministry of Labour have also been bes towed with certain powers and duties 
under these Statutes.  
 
14. Based on the views of both the Ministry of Rail ways and the Ministry of Labour & 
Employment, the Committee observes that both these Ministries are in agreement that the 
Ministry of Labour is the Appellate Authority, and in case, the unions/ federations are not 
satisfied with a rule framed by the Railways, they can take up the matter with the Labour 
Ministry.   The Committee is happy that there is no  dispute on the law side between these 
two  Ministries.   
 
15. The Committee is further in agreement with the views of the Ministry of Labour & 
Employment which states as under: 
‘The Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) who is hea ding the Central Industrial 
Relations Machinery (CIRM) who are responsible for maintaining harmonious relations 
between the Management and Unions should also be as sociated as a Member of the 
Committee.  The Ministry further suggests for inclu sion of a suitable representative from

recommend to have representatives of the recognized  Railway Unions/Federations in the 
High Power Committee to facilitate meaningful examination of issues which would, in the 
long run, ensure harmonious industrial relations in the Railways’.  
 

 The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Mi nistry of Railways and the 
Ministry of Labour & Employment should strive towards this goal in letter and spirit.

2.  While scrutinizing these Orders, the Committee note d that there was 
considerable time lag between issue  of Notificatio ns and their laying in some 
cases. The annexed statement also indicates the per iod of delay in cases where 
Notifications have not been laid as per the time sc hedule prescribed by the 
Committee. The Committee observed that of the total  352 Notifications that were 
delayed, there were 329 Notifications where no dela y statement was appended to. 
However, the bulk of delayed Notifications were fro m the Ministry of  Road 
Transport and Highways which comes to around 93.4% of the total delayed 
Notifications. 
 
The observations/recommendations of the Committee i n respect of the 
specific Ministries/Departments where delay in layi ng of Notifications has been 
noticed, are as follows: -  
 
(i) Ministry of Civil Aviation  
 
 The only one notification that the Ministry of Civ il Aviation (Sl. No. 8) 
have laid, was delayed by 8 months and no delay sta tement has been appended 
thereto. The Committee is concerned over the delay in laying  of the only  
Notification by the Ministry of Civil Aviation by  8 months. Further there is 
no delay statement appended to it citing details as  to what caused such delay. 
The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Minist ry to take care that 
such instances of delay do not recur in future and in case of any delay in 
laying, a delay statement should invariably be appended thereto. 
 

  
(ii) Ministry of Commerce and Industry (Department of Co mmerce and 
Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion)  
 
Ministry of   Commerce and Industry (Department of Commerce) have 
laid 3 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 9-11). Out of these,  two Notifications (Sl. No. 9-10) 
were delayed by 4 to 5 months and  there is no dela y statement appended to both 
of them. Whereas the Ministry of Commerce and Indus try  (Department of 
Industrial Policy & Promotion)  have laid 5 Notific ations  out of which  one was 
delayed by 7 months with no delay statement attached to it.  
 
The Committee expresses its unhappiness  over the d elay in laying of 
the above mentioned Notifications by the Ministry o f Commerce and 
Industry (Department of Commerce and Department of Industrial Policy & 
Promotion) resulting in a delay of  4 to 7 months. Further, no delay statement 
have been appended thereto  giving reasons for the delay. The Committee, 
therefore, would like  the Ministry to ensure that there are no delays in 
future and at all if these is a delay in laying, th ere should be a delay 
statement attached with it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
(iii) Ministry of Communications and Information Te chnology 
 
(a)   (Department of Electronics and Information Technology) 
  
 Ministry of Communications and Information Technology  (Department of  
Electronics and Information Technology)  have laid 10 Notifications (Sl. Nos. 17 
to 26).  Out of these, 6 Notifications have been de layed by 5 to 14 months. Only 
three  delayed Notifications (Sl. Nos. 17 and 19) w ere attached with delay 
statement  whereas the  other three Notifications ( Sl. Nos. 20 to 22) did not have 
any delay statement citing the exact reasons for de lay. The reason for delay given 
by the Ministry is as under:- 
  
 “The Electronics and IT Goods (Requirement of Comp ulsory Registration) 
Order, 2012 under the Bureau of India Standards Act , 1986 in English and Hindi 
versions, could not be laid on the Table of both th e Houses of parliament within 
the specified period as further amendments to these  Rules/ Subordinate 
Legislations were being issued. These documents are  now being laid on the Table 
of both the Houses of Parliament. 
 In future, all efforts will be made to ensure that  the documents are laid on 
the Table of the Houses by due date.” 

  
 The Committee regrets the delay in laying of Notifi cations due to 
amendments taking place. Instead of waiting for ove r a year to lay the 
notifications, the Ministry should have laid the no tifications on the first 
available opportunity. These amendments would have followed  suit. But the 
Ministry thought it would carry out the amendments and then  lay the 
Notifications. The Committee exhorts the Ministry t o lay the Notifications 
well in time in future at the first available opportunity, to avoid any delay. 
 
(b)  (Department of Telecommunications) 
 
Ministry of Communications and Information Technolo gy (Department of 
Telecommunications) have laid 7 Notifications (Sl. No. 27 to 33)  out  of which 
three Notifications were delayed by 3 to 11 months.  One of the Notification (Sl. 
No. 30) had a delay statement attached to it wherea s the other two did not have 
any delay statements with them. The reasons for del ay given by the Ministry are 
as under:- 
 
“The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) i s a statutory body 
set up under the Telecom Regulatory Authority of In dia Act, 1997. In exercise of 
the powers conferred upon it under section 36 of th e TRAI Act, 1997, the 
Authority may, by notification, makes regulations c onsistent with the Act. Under 
section 37 of the Act, the regulations notified by TRAI are required to be laid 
before each House of Parliament. 
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) in  exercise of the 
powers conferred by sub-section (1) of Section 36, read with sub-clauses (i), and 
(v) of clause (b) of sub-section (1) of Section 11 of the TRAI Act, 1997 notified 
“Standard of Quality of service (Duration of Advert isements in Television 
Channels) (Amendment) Regulation, 2013.” On receipt  of the copies of the 
gazette notification on 15 
th  April, 2013 from the Government of India Press, 
TRAI sent the Regulation to the Department on 16 th  April, 2013. Since  the 
subject matter of the Regulation i.e. television br oadcasting falls within the 
business allocated to the Ministry of Information &  Broadcasting as specified in 
the first schedule to the Govt. of India (Allocatio n of Business) Rules, so it was 
decided in the Department of Information and Broadcasting for laying of the same 
on the table of both Houses of Parliament by them. The same was forwarded to 
them on 25 th  April, 2013. 
Ministry of Information & Broadcasting has returned  the above said 
regulation to this department on 10 th  October, 2013, after the lapse of approximate 
6 months from the date of forwarding of said regula tion to them without laying or 
the same on the Table of the both Houses of Parliam ent. While returning of the 
regulation, the Ministry of Information & Broadcast ing has said that the said 
regulation is to be laid in both Houses of the Parl iament by the Department of 
Telecommunications as regulations of TRAI, notified  in the past, have not been 
referred to their Ministry for laying in the Houses of the Parliament. 

The matter was referred to Cabinet Secretariat, for  their advice, Reply 
from the Cabinet Secretariat has been received vide their O.M. No.1/21/112/2013-
Cab. Dated 13.12.2013. 
Accordingly, the Regulation titled “Standard of Qua lity of service 
(Duration of Advertisements in Television Channels)  (Amendment) Regulation, 
2013” is now being laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.” 
 
The Committee notes with surprise the reasons of de lay given by the 
Ministry of Communications and Information Technolo gy  (Department of  
Electronics and Information Technology and Departme nt of 
Telecommunications) where there was no clarity of j urisdiction  between the 
Ministries in laying of the Notifications. It respe cts that the Ministry  sticks 
to the schedule of laying of the Notifications as g iven in Committee’s 131 
st  
Report.

 Ministry of Corporate Affairs have laid 10 Notific ations (Sl. Nos. 41 to

respectively and there is no delay statement attached to either  of them. 
    
 The Committee notes with concern that two of the  N otifications laid 
by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs were not only delayed by three and  five 
months respectively  but also did not have any dela y statement attached to 
them. The Committee views it seriously  and reitera tes its recommendations  
as contained in its 135 
th  Report that in case there is delay in laying of 
Statutory Orders, the concerned Ministry/Department  should invariably 
append a delay statement. The Committee further imp resses upon the 
Ministry that it is their obligation towards the Pa rliament to invariably

The delay in laying these rules on the Tables of bo th the Houses of

st

th  March, 2013, copies of the Notifications

ones, the following recommendations, as contained i n its 131 
st 
, 135 
th 
, 152 
nd  ,

 “Orders required to be laid before the House shoul d be laid (i) if the 
House is not in Session, during the Session immedia tely following the date of 
publication of the Order in the Official Gazette an d (ii) if the House is in 
Session, on the date of the publication of the Orde r, during its continuance 
and in case the time lag between the date of public ation and the date of the 
closing of the Session is less than 15 clear days, before the expiry of the 
Session immediately following the said Session. All  the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India shoul d henceforth comply

 “The Committee has, time and again, emphasized tha t it is essential that

the Notifications being laid so as to apprise Parli ament of the causes of delay. 
The Committee desires all Ministries/Departments to  take a note of this, 
since the intention is that through the process of formulation of a delay 
statement, the Ministry is able to introspect, iden tify bottlenecks and devise 
remedial measures”. 
(135 th  Report)

 “In the opinion of the Committee, every notificati on should be assigned a 
distinctive number in order to give it a separate i dentity and similarly, no 
notification should be published/laid which does no t carry a notification 
number. The Committee expects all Ministries/Depart ments of Government 
of India to exercise caution in this regard. In cas e where there are more than 
one Notifications under a single file, the Ministri es/Departments should 
ensure that the file number on each notification sh ould be suitably 
distinguished from one another.” 
(152 
nd 
 Report) 
(Presented on 26 August 2004)  
 
 “In addition to the concern expressed by the Commi ttee over delay in 
laying of Notifications on the Table of the House, the Committee also express 
their deep concern over delay in framing of rules/r egulations under different 
Acts. The Committee in its 47 
th  report presented to the House on 14.9.1981 
has recommended that the rule-making process should be completed within a 
period of six months of the coming into force on an  Act. The Committee has 
further recommended that in case a Ministry is not able to adhere to this 
time limit, it should seek extension of time for co mpleting the rule-making 
process. The recommendation of the committee reads as follows:- 
 
  “The Committee feels that the rule-making process could well 
have been completed within the time limit of six mo nths which the 
Committee has laid down for making of rules under a n Act after 
coming into force of that Act. Where however, a Ministry does not find 
it possible to adhere to the time limit, they shoul d inform the 
Committee of the reasons why they cannot make rules  within the time 
limit and seek extension of time for completing the  rule-making 
process.” 
 The Committee is constrained to take note of the f act that the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India are n ot complying with the 
Committee’s recommendation to complete the process of framing of 
subordinate legislation contemplated under various Acts of Parliament 
within a period of six months. At the same time, th e Committee also does not 
receive requests for extension of time for completi ng the rule-making process 

in terms of its recommendations as above from most of the 
Ministries/Departments. The Committee takes a serio us note of the 
prevailing situation in which the Ministries/Depart ments are neither able to 
complete the task of framing rules/regulations unde r different Acts within 
the given six months’ period nor do they suo-motu  approach the Committee 
for seeking extension of time. The Committee furthe r notes that in order to 
ensure timely framing of rules/regulations it has t aken an initiative to 
monitor the progress of framing of subordinate legi slation in respect of all 
legislations brought about by different Ministries/ Departments of 
Government of India from the year 2003 onwards with  a view to ensure that 
the framing of subordinate legislation is not delay ed. The Committee, 
however, finds that the responses from the Ministri es/Departments have not 
been prompt in this monitoring exercise undertaken on behalf of the 
Committee. 
  
 In view of the above position, the Committee once again reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministries/Departments shou ld ensure putting in 
place subordinate legislation positively within a p eriod of six months of 
coming into force of the Act. The Committee further  recommends that in 
case the Ministry fails to meet with this deadline,  they should invariably 
approach the Committee for seeking extension of tim e. The Committee 
further recommends that in cases where the time lim it of six months is not 
adhered to, they should, while laying rules/regulat ions before the Parliament 
invariably lay a statement explaining the reasons w hy the framing of 
rules/regulations was delayed beyond six months so as to keep the Parliament 
apprised of the compliance of the Parliament’s mand ate  conferred upon the 
Executive.” 
(192 
nd 
 Report) 
(Presented on 26 August 2011)  
 
 
  Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are laid by dif ferent Ministries on 
the Table of the House under various provisions of parent Acts passed by 
Parliament. These Rules/ Regulations/Orders/bye-law s are published in the 
official Gazette before being laid on the Table of the House. Even after they 
are laid, it is very difficult to get access to these Notifications. The Committee 
recommends that such Rules/Regulations/Orders, etc. laid on the Table of the 
House should be invariably uploaded on the websites  of respective Ministries 
immediately on the same day when they have been lai d on the Table of the 
House, for information of Members of Parliament and  people at large for 
their easy access. 
201 
st  Report 
(Presented on 14 th  December, 2012)  
 
 

The Committee observes that the whole process of en acting laws is 
defeated if rules are not framed and laid on the Ta ble of the House in time.  
A reasonable delay could be understood but unjustif iably long delays should 
be avoided and the Ministries should work towards i mproving this position.   
The Committee hopes that Ministry would strive to k eep the delay to the 
minimum and take care that Notifications are laid o n the Table of the House 
at the first available opportunity after publication of Notifications. 
  
The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry that it is their 
responsibility to ensure that copies of the Notifications are printed timely and 
for this purpose, they need to evolve a suitable me chanism to ensure that 
notifications are laid in time.   The Committee is happy that the Ministry has 
evolved an internal mechanism/ procedure for this p urpose.  The Committee 
hopes that it would take action accordingly in orde r to comply with the 
prescribed schedule in the matter of laying of statutory Notifications. 
 
 
 
The Ministry must take appropriate step to remove l acuna, if any, 
administrative or otherwise causing such long delay  by being little proactive 
and prompt.  Further, the Ministries should take it  up with the Ministry of 
Urban Development for late receiving of printed copies of the Notification.

REPORT 
 
 
Report on the taking over of  Distance Education Council (DEC) of IGNOU by the 
University Grants Commission (UGC) through an administrative order in violation 
of IGNOU Act, 1985 and the Statutes framed thereunder  
 
The Distance Education Council (DEC), which had bee n created and was 
functioning under Indira Gandhi National Open Unive rsity (IGNOU), Act 1985 was 
abolished and its mandate was given to the Universi ty Grants Commission (UGC) and 
All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE) through an administrative order of the 
Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD) dated  29 December 2012 
(Annexure-I). This was  done  without making the necessary amendments in the IGNO U 
Act, 1985 which mandates IGNOU inter alia  to regulate distance education in the 
country.   DEC, which regulated distance education in the country, had come into 
existence as an authority of IGNOU under Statute 28   framed in exercise of powers 
conferred by Section 16 of the IGNOU Act, 1985.  No w, transferring the mandate given 
to IGNOU (read DEC) to the UGC & AICTE raises the following questions:  
(i)  whether an administrative order can undo something that was created 
under a law passed by Parliament;  
(ii)  whether this can be done without amending the IGNOU Act;  
(iii)  whether UGC and AICTE Acts provided for regulating the Open & 
Distance Learning (ODL) mode of education;  
(iv)   whether the Ministry was legally right in taking such a decision; and  
(v)  whether Ministry of Law was consulted before taking such a recourse?     
 
2. In order to examine and understand these issues,  the Committee requested he 
Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of Higher Education) to furnish 
its written comments vide  a D.O. letter dated 5 
 June 2013. The Ministry furnished their 
comments and clarifications on 25 June 2013 (Annexure-II) . 
 

3. The Ministry’s arguments for abolishing DEC and transferring its mandate - of 
regulating ODL system, to UGC & AICTE was basically  based on objections being 
raised by other Universities in this system.  Their  argument was how can one university 
(IGNOU) control or regulate the working of other un iversities in this system?  The 
Ministry informed that upto 2007, DEC used to give recognition to institutions offering 
general courses in the distance mode but during that year, DEC started giving recognition 
for technical programs also under the distance mode .  This was against the policy of the 
AICTE, which is responsible for maintaining standards in technical education, to conduct 
technical programs through regular (conventional) m ode only.  This created confusion as 
to who will regulate the technical education in the  ODL mode.  The Committee was 
informed that Delhi University had challenged the a uthority of the DEC to regulate their 
ODL programmes in the Delhi High Court.  The main issue before the Court was whether 
an authority of one university could regulate the o ther universities.  Unscrupulous 
institutions conducting ODL programmes started expl oiting this confusion to their 
commercial advantage, it was argued. 
 
4. The Ministry further informed that in view of th is, a 'Madhava Menon Committee' 
was constituted to suggest measures to regulate the standards of education being imparted 
through distance mode.  It recommended to create a separate regulatory authority - the 
Distance Education Council of India (DECI) for regu lating distance education by a 
separate Act of Parliament. The Ministry, however, did not accept the recommendation of 
bringing a separate Act for this purpose on the ple a that the 'Higher Education and 
Research Bill' was then pending in Parliament which  sought to subsume all such existing 
regulators into one authority. Therefore, the Minis try took a decision to let the existing 
regulators, viz. the UGC and AICTE to perform the r egulatory responsibilities for Open 
and Distance Learning (ODL) mode as well. 
 
5. The Ministry further argued that DEC, created th rough Statute 28, was dissolved 
with the approval of the Visitor i.e. the President  of India after following due procedure 
laid down in Section 25 of the IGNOU Act, 1985 as enumerated below: 
 

(i)  Minutes of the meeting regarding approval of the Ma dhava Menon 
Committee and taking over of DEC by UGC was forward ed to Chairmen 
AICTE, UGC and DEC for taking necessary action vide  the Ministry's 
letter dated 30.04.2012. 
 
(ii)  DEC accordingly discussed the issue regarding repea ling Statute 28 of 
IGNOU on 08.06.2012 and recommended to the Board of  Management 
(BOM), IGNOU to repeal Statute 28 framed under 16 o f the IGNOU Act, 
1985. 
 
(iii)  Board of Management (BOM), IGNOU considered the mat ter on 
28.07.2012, accepted the recommendation of DEC and decided to request 
the Visitor, i.e. the President of India to repeal Statute 28. 
 
(iv)  On receiving the approval of the Visitor  to repeal  Statute 28 of IGNOU, 
as required under the IGNOU Act, Notification dated  01.05.2013 was 
issued regarding repeal of Statute 28 of IGNOU Act. 
 
6. After considering the above facts and the issues  involved, the Committee heard 
the representatives of the Ministry of Human Resour ce Development (Department of 
Higher Education), Vice-Chancellor, IGNOU and Chair man, UGC for further 
clarifications in the matter on 30 July 2013. The M inistry was asked to clarify whether 
the mandate of regulating ODL mode of education can  be taken away from IGNOU 
simply by abolishing the DEC without amending the r elevant provisions of the IGNOU 
Act, 1985 for this purpose.  The Committee also ask ed about the specific Sections of an 
Act/Rule/Statute, etc. under which the said mandate  was shifted to UGC and AICTE.  
The Committee also wanted to know about the urgency  with which DEC was shifted to 
UGC without waiting till proper legislation in the matter was passed by Parliament.  
 
7. The Ministry could not give a convincing and leg ally tenable replies to the queries 
raised by the Committee.  It could not deny the fac t that mandate to regulate standards of 

education through distance mode still remained with  the IGNOU Act and that it did not 
cease to exist merely on the repeal of Statute 28 a bolishing DEC.  On the question as to 
which Section of UGC Act empowers UGC to regulate d istance education, Chairman, 
UGC informed the Committee that Section 12 of the U GC Act empowers UGC to 
regulate distance education which says, “It shall be the duty of the Commission to  take, in 
consultation with the Universities or other bodies concerned, all such steps as it may 
think fit for the promotion and co-ordination of Un iversity education and for the 
determination and maintenance of standards of teach ing, examination and research in 
Universities..”  . He further stated that the Ministry had issued a  Direction to UGC to take 
over DEC under Section 20(1) of UGC Act which said that the Central Government has 
the power to give Direction to the UGC, which is binding.   
 
8. As regards the urgency the Ministry stated that the Madhava Menon Committee 
was aware that passing of the Distance Education Council of India Bill as suggested by it, 
might take some time. It also felt that the positio n of UGC vis-à-vis IGNOU as a 
Regulator is stronger and more acceptable to the wh ole university system including the 
Open Universities.   Therefore, the Madhava Menon Committee recommended  that the 
Government should issue a policy direction/notifica tion to UGC for assuming the 
responsibilities of maintaining standards in ODL system and creating a DECI like interim 
authority for the purpose. That is the reason why D EC had been shifted to UGC as an 
interim arrangement.  
 
9. The Ministry also informed the Committee that as  the Higher Education and 
Research Bill was unlikely to be cleared by Parliam ent, a decision had then been taken to 
have a separate legislative enactment as suggested by the Menon Committee for setting 
up of Distance Education Council of India.  They sa id that the DECI Bill had been 
prepared.  Thereafter, a Cabinet Note would be prep ared and the opinion of the 
Legislative Department would be taken before the Bill is introduced in Parliament.  
 
10. On the Committee’s query in regard to regulatin g technical education in distance 
mode, the Ministry clarified that even earlier when  the regulation of distance education 

was with DEC under IGNOU, it was only for general e ducation and that technical 
education was regulated by AICTE only.  An Order is sued by the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development on 29  December 2012 gave Direction to both UGC and AICTE to 
regulate distance education and that AICTE shall look at ODL for technical education. 
 
11. The Committee was further informed that DEC did  not go out of existence 
because of its disassociation with IGNOU; it will b e very much in existence, performing 
its current duties, but it will do so under the UGC  till the new arrangement could be 
made.   
 
12. The Committee again heard the Vice-Chancellor, IGNOU and Chairman, UGC 
for further clarifications in the matter on 31 Janu ary 2014. During the meeting, Vice-
Chancellor, IGNOU stated that IGNOU was for making DEC an independent body. 
Chairman, UGC argued that prior to 1991, the entire  higher education was regulated by 
UGC which had the mandate to maintain standards of teaching, examinations and 
research in higher education. Chairman, UGC replied  that under Section 20(1) of UGC 
Act, the Ministry can issue Directions and argued t hat the Ministry is within its mandate 
to issue Directions to UGC and UGC has also within its ambit to regulate distance 
education. Chairman, UGC further stated that he was  happy about the transfer of DEC to 
UGC and that he had already put a system in place f or this purpose.   He claimed that 
they had cleared all pending cases before DEC after  the work was transferred to them in 
December, 2012.  He also informed the Committee tha t previously, DEC was regulated 
through guidelines.  But now, they had come up with  Regulations which had been sent to 
the Ministry of Human Resource Development for its concurrence. Once the concurrence 
of the Ministry is received, the Regulations would be notified. 
 
13. The Chairman, UGC expressed his opinion that th ere was no need to have another 
regulatory authority.  He was of the view that inst ead of creating a large number of 
regulatory bodies, we can have only one authority, an overarching body in the country for 
the purposes of regulating higher education, under which there could be a number of 
instruments to take care of the different facets of  education.  In conclusion, the 

Committee observed that a faux pas  was made by the Ministry of HRD by hurriedly 
repealing DEC and transferring its work to UGC by a n Executive Order and 
IGNOU did not put any kind of formal resistance to this.  The Committee was of the 
view that these questions would be best answered by  the Ministry of HRD. 
Accordingly, it decided to hear the Ministry of HRD  again before reporting the 
matter to the House. 
 
14. The Committee thereafter heard the Secretary, M inistry of Human Resource 
Development (Department of Higher Education) on the  matter on 28 February 2014. On 
the Committee’s query as to why a new legislation w as not brought before Parliament, 
the Secretary stated that the National Council for Higher Education and Research Bill to 
create one umbrella regulator for all educational i nstitutions has been pending before 
Parliament for the last four years. Due to this, he  submitted that it would not have been 
proper to bring in legislation affecting one partic ular sector of education.    He assured 
the Committee that the Ministry is committed to cre ating an independent Distance 
Education Council of India (DECI) by separate legis lation as recommended by the 
Madhava Menon Committee and that the Bill will be b rought before Parliament.  When 
the Committee wanted to know the time-frame by whic h this will be done, the Secretary 
replied that the Bill should be ready within three months to be vetted by the Law Ministry 
which will be taken to the Cabinet, thereafter. 
 
15. Despite the assurance given by the Secretary, D epartment of Higher Education, 
the Committee was not informed about the status in the matter nor was the Bill since been 
introduced in Parliament. Accordingly, D.O. letter was issued to the Secretary, 
Department of Higher Education on 23 September 2014  to furnish a status report 
regarding the Bill as assured to the Committee. In response, the Ministry, vide  their letter 
dated 15 October 2014 stated that draft Cabinet Note and draft Bill on Distance 
Education Council of India (DECI) have been prepare d and the concerned file is 
under submission of the Human Resources Minister (H RM). Upon approval of the 
same by HRM, further necessary action regarding seeking approval of Cabinet shall 
be taken . 

  
 
 
COMMITTEE’S OBSERVATIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
 
16. The Committee after perusing the papers, docume nts, etc. furnished by the 
Ministry; facts and clarifications given during ora l evidences by the Ministry, the 
UGC and IGNOU feels that the demand of other ODL Un iversities to take DEC out 
from IGNOU fold was well taken.  Parliament, when I GNOU Act was passed in 
1985 for ODL system, had thought it prudent to give  the regulatory powers also to 
IGNOU, because the distance mode of education at th at time was at a rudimentary 
stage.  But in view of vast expansion of ODL system  during all these years, the 
Committee is of the view that might involve a confl ict of interest, therefore, DEC 
may be taken out of IGNOU fold and to provide it st atus of independent regulatory 
body through a separate Act of Parliament on the li nes of UGC and AICTE as they 
have their own Acts. 
 
17. The Committee is happy that the Ministry ultima tely has decided to take 
DEC out of the IGNOU but it expresses its serious r eservation about the manner in 
which DEC has been transfeered to UGC by an adminis trative order.  The 
Committee hastens to add that it does not have any reservation about the manner in 
which the DEC was abolished; it had been done as pe r the procedure laid down in 
the IGNOU Act and Statutes made thereunder. 
 
UGC and ODL 
 
18. The Committee is of the considered opinion that  transferring DEC and its 
mandate to the UGC and AICTE is legally untenable.  It also feels that abolition of 
DEC was done with undue haste for which no convinci ng explanation could be 
furnished, either by the Ministry or by the UGC.   
 

19. The Committee notes that nowhere in the UGC Act  it is specifically 
mentioned that UGC has the power to regulate distan ce education also.  The 
Committee feels that interpreting Section 12 of UGC  Act, 1956 to include distance 
education as well as fallacious and untenable. The Committee also notes that Section 
20(1) of the UGC Act only gives the Ministry the po wer to issue Directions which 
can never be extended to override the powers grante d to IGNOU (for regulating 
distance education) through IGNOU Act passed by Parliament. 
 
20. In this regard, the Committee would like to quo te the Madhava Menon 
Committee Report, paragraph no. 6.6, page 59 which says: 
 
"The provisions of the IGNOU Act suggest that the P arliament intended, 
for the purpose of regulatory arrangements, to trea t higher education 
through open and distance learning differently from  the conventional 
university system, in view of its unique characteri stics.  Therefore, while 
setting up a separate university, IGNOU, for impart ing higher education 
through ODL system, the Act also gave the responsib ility of 
development, coordination and determination of stan dards in the Open 
and Distance Education system to it, "notwithstandi ng anything 
contained in any other law for the time being in fo rce".  Accordingly, the 
IGNOU established the Distance Education Council in  the year 1991 to 
discharge the responsibilities as a Regulator of the ODL system".  
 
21. It is evident that while ODL system may have be en with UGC before, but the 
position changed after DEC was created in 1991 unde r IGNOU Act passed in 1985.  
To buttress this position, the Committee would furt her like to refer to paragraphs 
3.2, page 19 of the Menon Committee Report which al so argues that "with the 
enactment of the IGNOU Act, the legal position in r espect of regulation of ODL 
system changed.  IGNOU, besides being a University of Open and Distance 
Learning, was also entrusted with the responsibilit y of laying down norms and 

maintaining standards of distance education system in the country which is evident 
from the preamble" of the Act and its Sections 4 and 5 (2) as well.   
 
22. Therefore, the Ministry's contention that UGC h ad the powers to regulate 
higher education in general encompasses power to re gulate ODL as well is basically 
flawed.  This argument may have been acceptable bef ore the IGNOU was given 
power to regulate ODL.  Thus, the power to regulate ODL that may have been there 
in other law, ceased to exist after IGNOU Act came into being. 
 
AICTE and ODL 
 
23. As regards AICTE, the Committee notes that even  AICTE Act, 1987 does not 
specifically provide for regulating distance educat ion programmes.  A Notification 
(No. 44 of March 1995) of the MHRD has made approva l of DEC necessary for 
degrees awarded through distance education by unive rsities/institutions of national 
importance and wherever necessary AICTE also supported this interpretation.  . 
 
24. The Committee, in view of the nature and signif icance of technical education 
and the competitive advantage that India enjoys in this field world over, is also of 
the view that there should not be any confusion and  dilution regarding enforcement 
of the specifications/standards of technical educat ion in the country.  Besides, 
excluding technical education altogether from the O DL system may not be a 
desirable thing in view of its outreach, affordabil ity and popularity.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to  consider this aspect while 
drafting DECI Bill and also amending relevant provi sions of AICTE Act, if 
necessary.     
 
25. The Committee finds that it is very clear from the Preamble and Sections 4, 
5(2) & 24(j) of IGNOU Act, 1985 as well as AICTE Ac t and UGC Act that IGNOU  
as on date remains the sole authority for regulatin g distance education in the 
country and power of UGC and AICTE in this regard m ight be implied not 

expressed.  In other words, expressed provisions of  a law shall necessarily override 
the implied aspect of another law.  If there was a justifiable need and reason for 
transferring this responsibility from IGNOU to UGC & AICTE, it should have been 
done by making necessary amendments in IGNOU Act and by a separate enactment 
and not certainly through an administrative order. The Committee would like to 
reiterate that administrative orders cannot override a law passed by Parliament and 
assented to by the President of India.  The Committ ee accordingly recommends that 
while preparing DECI Bill, the IGNOU Act, 1985 shou ld be amended by 
deleting/amending the provisions which mandate IGNO U to regulate distance 
education such as the Preamble and Sections 4, 5(2)  & 24(j) of the Act.  This has 
been suggested by the Menon Committee as well that was set up by the Ministry. 
 
26. The Committee welcomes the assurance given by t he Secretary, Department 
of Higher Education before the Committee on 28 Febr uary 2014 that the Ministry is 
committed for creating an independent Distance Education Council of India (DECI) 
through a separate legislation and the time-frame o f three months within which the 
Bill would be ready for the same. The Committee, ho wever, found that the Bill for 
creation of DECI could be introduced in Parliament within the time frame given by 
the Ministry. The Committee notes that in response  to a D.O. letter from the 
Committee Secretariat in September, 2014, Ministry stated that  draft Cabinet Note 
and draft Bill on Distance Education Council of Ind ia (DECI) had been prepared 
and the concerned file was under submission of the Human Resources Minister 
(HRM) and that upon approval of the same by HRM, fu rther necessary action 
regarding seeking approval of Cabinet shall be take n accordingly. The Committee 
finds that there is apparent reluctance on the part  of the Ministry to bring a 
separate legislation for creating DECI for reasons better known to it.   The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the process should be expedited and the Bill 
should be introduced in Parliament at the earliest.   
 
27. It may be pointed out that the Parliamentary St anding Committee on HRD 
which was considering the Bill to constitute an ove r-arching body subsuming all the 

Regulators of Higher Education had submitted its re port rejecting the proposed 
body in December 2012 i.e.  long before the 25 June 2013 when the Ministry had  
informed this Committee that it was not bringing an y Bill for creating DECI on the 
ground that the former was pending before HRD Stand ing Committee.  The 
Ministry needs to clarify its position in this regard.      
 
28. Now, we have come to a situation where DEC has been abolished and its 
powers are being exercised by UGC and AICTE the ver y legal basis of which is 
under question.  The Ministry says that DEC in actu al practice, will not cease to 
exist after its disassociation with IGNOU; it will continue to perform its current 
duties but under UGC till the alternate arrangement is made.  It further complicates 
the situation in respect of technical education whi ch is under the AICTE.  The 
Committee feels that the new arrangement will create further confusion between the 
UGC (read DEC) and AICTE.  The Committee, therefore , is of the opinion that 
there should be a single regulator for distance edu cation-whether technical or 
general. The Committee hopes that the proposed Bill  would give the mandate of 
regulating all forms of distance education in the hands of DECI only. 
 
29. The Committee is concerned that the interests a nd rights of the employees of 
the erstwhile DEC of IGNOU may be adversely impacte d through their shifting 
from IGNOU to UGC. The Committee, therefore, urges the Ministry to ensure that 
the interests and rights of the employees of the er stwhile DEC are protected and 
that they are not adversely impacted/unduly disadva ntaged as a result of this 
shifting of DEC and also when the proposed DECI comes into being.   
 
30. The Committee questions both the manner as well  as urgency with which 
DEC was abolished and its mandate was shifted/trans ferred to UGC and AICTE. 
The Committee feels that as advised by the experts,  members of the DEC, VCs of 
the open universities and Members of Board of Manag ement of IGNOU, DEC could 
have remained with IGNOU until the DECI was set up by an independent Act of 
Parliament.  It is evident from the Minutes of the DEC on 27 
 May 2012 in which 

despite larger opinion being against doing this, it  passed a Resolution for deletion of 
Statute 28.   
 
31. While going through the minutes of the meeting of the Distance Education 
Council dated 8 June 2012 and that of the Board of Management, IGNOU dated 19 
 
September 2012, the Committee observed that there w ere two prominent views 
which were echoed by most of the Members, viz. (i) it would be appropriate if DEC 
is made an independent regulator rather than shifti ng it under the UGC and (ii) 
DEC should continue under IGNOU in the present set up. Some Members of DEC 
even raised the question on the ability of UGC to p erform such a role for DEC 
which was being performed by IGNOU for it and cauti oned against mixing of 
regulation of conventional and ODL systems which ar e two different modes of 
imparting education. The Chairman of DEC also stres sed to make DEC as an 
independent regulator for all practical purposes ra ther than shifting it to 
UGC/AICTE. 
 
32. The Committee also took note of the resolution passed by the Vice-
Chancellors of State Open Universities (SOUs) held on 18 September 2012 wherein 
they resolved that DEC should be made an independen t regulatory body and till 
such time it becomes an independent regulator, status quo  may be maintained. The 
Committee wondered how despite all opposition for s hifting of DEC to UGC, DEC/ 
Board of Management, IGNOU reached the resolution t o recommend the shifting of 
DEC to UGC.
